- - - The love of excellence should be above the love of ex- celling. If you should nappen to want your ears pierced, just pinch the baby. " He:is a man of moist habits," is the modest way of saying 'a man is aldrunkard. s -The love of glory can only create a hero: the contempt of it creates a great man. In love we grow acquainted because we are already attached; in:friendship we must know each other before we love. There are two things to which we never grow accus- tomed—the ravages] of time and the injustice of our fellow-men. "What is sweeter than to have a friend you can trust?" askedi Sawkins. "To have a friend who will trust you," replied Dawkins. On a certain Scotch earl—a notoriously dull man—de- manding the Order of the Thisile, Lord Melbourne exclaimed, "Give the Thistle to—. Why, he'd eat it!" A dentist with toothache is a spectacle as rare as it is gratifying. It comes, perhaps, but once in a lifetime, but it brings with it a fragrance that remains for years.. Stationmaster (to suspicious-looking lady, aged, who had just entered a first-class compartment): "Are you first-class, mans?" Aged lady: "Yes, thank you; how are you ? " "Can you forgive me and love me still," said the new- made bride, "when I confess that my teeth are—arti- ficial?" "Thank goodness," cried the groom, as he snatched off his wig, "now I can cool my head!" The baseness, stupidity, folly, injustice, sufferings, and wreck this world everywhere presents are always a ' splendid challenge to strength, diligence, endurance, faith, wisdom—to all sublime and manly qualities. A sailor, being asked how he liked his bride, is re- ported to have remarked : "Why, d'ye see, I took her to be only one-half of me, as the parson says, but, dash me, if she isn't twice as much as I. lam only a tar— she's a tartar." She: "Before we were married you promised that my path through life should be strewn with roses; and now I have to sit up nights and darn stockings." He: "You -don't want to walk on roses barefooted, do you! You'd -get thorns in your feet." He who blames himself takes a by-road to praise, and, like the rower, turns his back to the place whither he edesires to go. He would be irritated if what he said against; himself was believed, but from a principle of pride he desires to appear humble. - "Edward, why do I hear that you disobeyed your grandmother, who told you just now not to jump down these steps ?" "Grandma didn't tell me not to, papa: she only said, I wouldn't jump down those steps, boys.' And I shouldn't think she would—an old lady like her." Archdeacon Stretch, of Victoria, was oiacelbeing bothered by a clerical bore, named Cass. Mr. Cass had one fad—that the great Napoleon was of scriptural descent lPressed for his reasons, he explained that "Napoleon" with the initial letter cut off gave Apoleon," or "Appolyon," a name prominent in Revelation. " replied the Archdeacon, "your own name 'Gags,' with the initial letter cut off, gives 'Ass,' but there's no revelation in that." Lord Chelmstord was so stately in his presence and so dignified in his appearance that many years ago, when be was a younger man and more erect of carriage, he was accosted in the street by a hurried individual, who, mistaking him for some acquaintance, elapsed him by the hand, exclaiming, "flow are you, Mr. Smith?" Sir Frederick Thesiger, as he then was, drew himself up, and, gazing coldly on his questioner, replied, "Sir, do I look like a person of the name of Smith?" and :passed gravely on. All pilgrims to Rome know Spithover's book shop in the Piazzi di Spagna. Now Spithover is the most learned of bibliopoles. You must go thither if you need artistic a,nd archreological works of the profoundest research and erudition. But one of the ladies in a tourist's party only wanted the lively travels in America of Mr. "Max O'Rell," and she asked for the book at Spithover's. There came in a deep guttural voice—an Ang,lo-German voice—from a spectacled clerk behind a desk to this effect, "Marcus Aurelius cos neffer in to Unidted Statutes." HE Fornen OUT.—It is not easy to tell a self-con- ceited man how he is regarded, but now and then some one proves equal to the task. During the civil war a man, great in his own eyes, was, by some influence, ap- pointed a brigadier-general. His sense or his own im- portance was at once greatly increased. He could hardly speak of anything else but his new dignity. Meet- ing a "homespun' Yankee one day, he accosted him thus--" Well, Jim, I suppose you know I have been ap- pointed brigadier-general ?" "Yes," said Jim, "1 heerd so." "Well, what do folks say about it?" "Their don't say nothin," replied truthful James. "'they jest laugh." Ex-Governor Cornell, of New York, tells a good story at his own expense. It seems that when in office at Albany he would sometimes return home late at night, after his wife had retired, and when she asked him what time it was would answer, "About 12, or a little after midnight." One evening, instead of making the inquiry, she said. "Alonzo, I wish you would stop that clock; I cannot sleep for its noise." All unsuspicious. he stopped the pendulum. In the morning, while dressing, Mrs. Cornell inquired, artlessly, "Oh, by the way, what time did you get home ?" About midnight." " Alonzo, I look at that clock !" The hands of the clock pointed tol 2 30. The Governor was crushed. AMUSEMENTS or INVENTORS.—Crompton. the inventor of the mule-spinning process, found relaxation from his more seriousipursuits in playing the fiddle, and became a sufficient master of the instrument to be able to accept an engagement in the hand of the Bolton Theatre at a ' time when he was wanting funds for his experiments. This service brought him in eighteen-pence a night, and was of great assistance to him! Richard Trevithick. the Cornish engineer and inventor, who did so much towards the perfecting of ' the locomotive, amused him- self with many inventive dreams that were never rear sed. One of them is worth alluding to at the present time as being a sort of a foreshadowing of the Eiffel Tower. Trevithick's idea was to erect a national monument in honour of the Reform Bill, to take the shape of a stupen- pus eircUlar column of cast iron, gilt, to be 1,000 feet high, 100 feet in diameter at the base, and 12 feet at the top, to weigh 6,000 tons, and to cost £8),000. This monumental column was to be "symbolical of the beauty - and strength and unaffected grandeur of the British Constitution." Beyond this, there was to be a central tube, 10 feet in diameter, for conveying passengers up - and down, driven by a steam engine. Two months after . giving this idea to his Countrymen, he died at Dartford, -'penniless, without any relation at hand to perform the st sad offices for him.—Caesell's Saturday journal. • WHAT BECOMES OF THE WASTR—SOOIO years ago, a r t of universal provider in a, populous Lancashire t05..71 anneuiaced by placard and advertisement that he had Temeheaea fifty tons of coal from a neighbouring leit, and that he would sell it for exactly what he had paid for it—namely, fivepence per cwt. The local coal dealers were frantic, and wondered long and seriously where the cost of advertising would come from, to say -nothing of the return for time and trouble. To this -day, we believe, they are as much in the dark a.s ever. Here, however, is the secret, as it was told to the writer By the man himself. He had first of all bought for a mere song, he said, a set of roundabouts, and had had them erected in his yard. Knowing full well that if he could only get children into the yard, his speculation would be patronised, tie hit upon the device of selling coal upon the terms mentioned. His stock went like wild- fire. Flocks of children took away the coal in little waggons, and, having seen the roundabouts, asked their mothers for coppers, so that they could have a ride when they re- turned. The result was precisely what the shrewd man had anticipated ; he s,mined a reputation for cheapness, and at the same time indirectly made a profit on his teal. The crowning stroke, however, was his accept- ance of all sorts of waste in return for rides; for more than once he made a profit of aid. by ,a transaction of this sort. When his stock ot reCuse became troublesome, he had it sorted into heaps. Most of it was afterwards re-manufactured in tie neighbourhood. and was returned to his shop in the shape of useful household articles. "Look there I" said the man, in conClusion, pointing with justifiable pride to a row of copper kettles haneing from the roof, "some of the copper I got for halfpenny rides is in those kettles !" This transaction was in its way quite as smart as that of the trailesmsn who had the sagacity to buy the iron from if the piles of old London Bridge, and convert it (n, tvrithstanding that it had lain for centuries under water) into some of the STIPA sur- gical instruments of the day.—From Cassell's Saturday' Journal tor January. THE BEST VALENTINE. "Ea! ha!" said the eartn, one fair spring day, As under the noon-tide sun she lay, For each little merry maiden mine We'll twine and wreath a sweet valentine." The birdies made of the words a song. The breezes bore the glad sounds along, And the bleating lambs and the lowing kine, All echoed but one word—" valentine." Ho! ho! how the tree-tops shook with fun, , And laughed to see all the sunbeams run , With golden fingers to wreath and twine For each little maid a valentine. Dear little sunbeams, how they toil, While flowers peep forth fro:n the yielding soil! What delicate tints and hues combine All, all for a wee maid's valentine! Twining and weaving the live-long day; ' Nay, not at eve do the labours stay— Then dew-drops fall, and the stars must shine; A wondrous thing is a valentine! Garland of violets, white and blue, Wreaths of wild flowers, dripping with dew, The crocus, daisy, all intertwine. For this is a world-wide valentine. " Valentines ! valentines!" so shouts the earth, "Free without money, priceless their worth, Sweetness and purity—maidens mine, Take to your heart this best valentine." —Little Folks Magazine.
HOW JOHNNY DICK LEARNED THE EIGHTH COMMANDMENT.

I was a gey wee shaver when it happened, but I'll tell ye a' aboot it. I was comin' hame frae the schule ae efternoon —me an' anither big lassie—an' juist as we cam' up by the turn o' the road whar Robin Tamson's farm is, the big lassie turns roond to me, and quo' she—

"I'll hae a turnip." " Sae will I," says I. Sae we baith loupit the sheuch an' owre the dyke into the turnip field. She waled ane o' the biggest, an' so did I, an' I sat doon on my hunkers to peel mine wi' my grand big gully knife, an' had jist got the first bite into my month when I lookit up, an' wha was there standin' foment me but my mither I Hoc) she cam there, and whar she cam' frae, I couldna tell, an' she never tell't me ;but there she was.

She lookit atrauCht into my face, an' says she, slowly " Johnny Dick, has ye a pocket naipkin? If ye hae, spread it doon, an' gether up the thing ye're eatin', an' the peelin's an' the shaws, an' everything connectit wi't an' come yer wa's wi' me." I was sae ta'en I couldna speak no ae word, but just gethered a' up as fast as I could, an' stood on my feet to see what was comin' next. My mither didna keep me lang waitin' ; she jist took a grup o' me my the lug, an' led me doon by the side o' the turnip field. Doon, doon we geed— wi' my pocket haukey by the four corners in my right hand, an' my mither wi' a guid grup o" my left lug. As I hae said, we gaed doon an' doon the field. It was the langest field that ever I tramped, either afore or since. I thocht we wad never get to the bottom o't, an' the warst o't was I didna ken whar she was leadin' me to. Mebbe thinks Ito droon me in the dam for takiu' the turnip; mebbe to feed me into the threshing machine in the next field. "Wed, at brag last we got to the end of the turnip field, an' turnin' roond an' along an' up to the farm hoose I began noo to hae a glimmer o' what was likely to happen. Robin Tamson, the farmer, was an unco nice man —indeed, he was jist a reel nice man—everybody like, him, but somehoo cc ither I wasna carin' to see him that day, nor yet to gang near whaur he leered; but faith, my mither led me bo the lug as straucht as the craw flees up. to the farm /moose. When we got there the dtor was standin' wide open, an' Robin an' his wife ha the kitchen lookin' as if they had seen us cominr, but couldrra under- stand the reason for oor visit. We waukit richt in—my mither an' rae—an' as soon as we got into the kitcten she pointed to the pocket naipkin, an' signed me to spread it dem on the floor; and then she lookit isa the farmer, an' quo' she— "Mr. Tamson, here's a thief I hoe brocht to ye wha has been stealin' turnips oot o'"yer field; an' stealin's a crime, ye ken, that maun be punished, sae ye can jile him if ye like ; " them she turned aboot an' vanished oot o' the door, leavin' me standin' tremblin' a' by mysel' on the middleo' the kitchen floor, we my pocket naipkin spread not at my tees, an' the tnrnip au' a' belanginr to it inside o't. I durstna look up, but just waited an' waited wir a deid wecht at my heart like to sink me into the. grand. Mr. Tamson, as my mither ca'ed him, drew along breath, an' quo' he— Johny Dick, my lad, since ye has made restitution, an' brocht back the turnip ye. stole; I'll no jile ye ; but," quo' he, " I wad just like to pit stealin' oot o' yer head, an, I'm thinkin" if ye• had a guid clink o' my big stick owre yer hurdles ye wadna meddle wi' my turnips again, or wi' ocht else that belongs to ither folk. Stand there," quo he, "till I fetch my big stick," an' wi' that he gaed' ben the hoose. The mistress rookit at me awfu' pleasant like, an' grippin' me by the arm, she said in a whisper, " Rin, 'addle, rin for yer fife afore he col back." Sae oot at the door 1 shot like an arrow; but there was my mither standin'on the doorsteps. an' she jist grippit me by the oxter before I could get past her, an' led me home. That was anither weary tramp„ I can tell ye ; but at last we got to oor aim lame. Then my m ither says to me, says she— "Johnny Dick, gang away up, tae yer bed, an' think ye has gotten at the supper yell get the xiicht not o' yon tnrnip. ' Sae air I had to gang. an' I hay lang,lang ; an' the upshot o' my thochts was this, that I had gone twice through the. Catechism free beginning to end, the Ten Commandments, wit the" Reasons Annexedian' never till that day did I fairly under- stand the nreanin'o'the words o' the Eighth Cam- mandment—" Thom shalt net steal.'

a gridiron to iron a shirt. "It is really very odd, my dear I" said an (Ad lady, orie -very hot day, to her friend. "I can't bear the heat in summer, and in winter I love it." It your son asks something of you which you know ought not to be granted, do not hesitate to say " No. ' It is a wise father, says the proverb, who no's his own son.
"Smelling bottles cause red noses and watery eyes," says a doctor. That may perhaps scare the
la'die's a little, but it is a fact that men with extra
cochineal noses seldom smell bottles. They don't
wait to smell.
AN lowa editor wrote an obituary on one of his subscribers, at the request of his widow, in which
he inadvertently spoke of the deceased having gone to a "far happier home." And the fastidious

mourner was angry. LADY—" Why did you leave your last place? ' Servant—" Well, you see, mum, I had to pay for all my breakages, and as they came to more than my wages, yer see, mum, it was a kind of impogission that I couldn't stand."
A FRNNCH investigator has discovered that the character of a person's dream depends in a great measure on which side the sleeper lies. The dreams cf a lawyer, then, who habitually lies on both sides,
. „ . must be very much mixed. , "My papa's a great man, he is. He is an office- holder." "What's his office, then 2" "He's . a
building inspector." "I'd think that would be awful dangerous going around unsafe buildings." "Oh, no. He don't go near 'em till after they fall down."

A MISTRESS Who had just hired a new cook made a tour of inspection after she had kept her a week, and found a policeman locked up in the pantry. "How did this man get here 7" asked the lady severely. "I'm sure I dou't know," answered the girl; "he must have been left over by the old cook." MRS. Die BLANK (bride of a year)—" I don't see what has changed you so, George." George—"! have not changed." "You have. You treat me now as any ordinary man treats his wife. There was a time when I was not a mere companion.

was a pet." "Yes, dear; but then you never got in a pet. HIGH SCHOOL GIRL (to Uncle James, a farmer)— "Do you like living on a farm, Uncle James ? " Uncle James—"? suppose it is nice enough in the glad summer time, but to to go out in the cold and snow to gather winter apples and harvest win- ter wheat I inagine might be anything but pleas- ant." _ _ .

"HAVE you anything to say " asked Justice Noonan of a prisoner upon whom he was about to pass sentence. ".Yes, judge," was the reply of the prisoner, whose penalty had been assessed at imprisonment for life, "I think that the time wasted in making that long winded speech by that young' galoot you appointed to defend me, ought to be taken out of my sentence."

A GREEN sportsman tried to shoot a sparrow with an old Queen Anne. musket. When he fired, the bird, with a chirrup 417 two, flew away unconcerned; in the foreground, and the marksman was swiftly and noiselessly laid OM his spine in the background. Picking himself up, and shaking his fist at the bird, he exclaimed: "Be jabers I ye wouldn't a chirruped' if you'd been at this end of the gun." THE celebrated Dr. Abernethy hated the egotistic garrulity of people who.came to consult him. A lady on one occasion entered his consulting-room, and put before him an injured finger without saying a word. In silence Abernethy dressed the wound, and the lady instantly and silently put the usual fee on the table and retired. In a few days she returned, and held out her finger free from band- ages and perfectly healed. "Well?" was Abcrnethy's monosyllabic inquiry. "Well," was the lady's equally brief answer. 'Upon my word, madam," exclaimed the delighted`surgeon, "you are the most sensible woman I ever met with "

SONE years ago a lady engaged a domestic ser- vant from the Highlands. In the evening the lady wanted supper brought in, so she rang the bell. Getting no answer, she repeated the sum- mons, but with the same effect. She then pro- ceeded to the kitchen, where, to lier amazement, she found her servant almost com ulsed with 1 laughter. She pointed to the bell and exclaimed —"As eure's I leeve F Lever touched it, an' it 's I waggin' yet!" "Do they miss me home, do they miss me?" soared the vocalist, in a- falsetto bass tremulo. Before he could proceed further, a fellow in the gallery remarked, "Yes, I think they do. As I came by, the old man was snoring in his chair, and the deg was fast asleen before the fire, and the old woman was telling the cat that it was the first quiet morpent she'd seen for a week. Yes, sir; they missed you by a large majority." The vocalist did net finish his son but rushed out into the silent night. • OLD Mr. Benningtom(in art gallery)—" Who did you say painted it ?" Dealer—" Rubens." Old Mr. Bennington—" What is-it worth 9" Dealer—" Five hundred pounds." Cal Mr. Bennington—" Five hundred what 7" Dealer—" Pounds." Old Mr. Ben- nington—" For one of 'ern 7" Dealer—" Yes." Old 'Mr. Bennington—" Mat's the man's name what painted it, did you say 7" Dealer—" Rubens." Old 'Mr. Thennington—" Will, give me his address, an' tll bet you the price ef a first-class frame that I kin git him to paint one jes? like, it for half the money." TREATRICAL MANAGER (breathlessly)—" Are you , busy r Drarnatist--" Not very.* "Well, everybody is talking about a book called 'Robert Elsmere' and I want a dramatisation of it right away. Can you do it r "Dramatise 'Robert Elsmere 7"" that's it. Work inr a,few elopements and murders and that sort of thing, you know, and a prairie fire and :a cyclone—got the machinery all ready—and pub in a low comedy part for Jinks ; he's the best stage Irishman in the country, you know, and last week I got two of the funniest trick mules you ever saw. Big bargain. too. Work them in somehow. Well, ta ta I I'm fur, a hurry. See you later."' A DierniGIJISHMI divine of unusually solemn and- Inapressive appearance went out to a country town not long ago to. lecture. He arrived early in the afternoon, and aIL the town, of course, spotted hins. within five mhintes as a very great and very saintly man. He went Into an apothecary's shop, and, im tones that froze•the young blood of the shopman,, • said—" Young—man—do—yon—smoke 7 " "Y— -yes, sir," said the trembling clerk; " Pm sorry, bat I learned the habit young and haven't been able to quit it yet." "-Then," said the great divine, with- out the movement of a muscle or the-- abatement of a shade of tho, awful solemnity of his voice, "can you tell me where I can get a good cigar?" - - -

TUB height of meanness was rettabed by them= who, having been rescued from a watery grave in the Serpentine daring the skating season, and duly brought round. after much trouble, in the Royal Humane Society's receiving house, promptly stole the grappling irons as he left the place and sold them for old metal on his way home! Another defini- tion asserts that the height of meanness consists giving a blind man a bad shilling and taking full change for it cot of his hat. 3ut the Woodbridge Gazetas now claims for that town the credit of poss- essing the meanest man in the person of a miserly yeoman who refused to allow his daughter to receive a sealskin jacket from her uncle as a present because, forsooth, he could not afford to pay for the camphor which would be needed to keep the moths out of it during the winter. A Trona suddenly appeared before a peasan one day and asked for a certificate of character explaining that he desired it to help him better his fortunes. 'But what can I say good of you]' protested the peasant. "Why, man, I 'ye had a dozen chances to down your whole family, but have never even bitten one!" Moral—We don't know how thankful we ought to be to the burglars will don't burgle. "ARE your domestic relations agreeable 7" was the queFtion put to an unhappy looking specimen of humanity. "Oh, my domestic relations are all right," was the reply; "it is my wife's relations that are causing Axe trouble." A NEVADI politicitin was elected on the merits of a single speech, the effect of which was described as " absolutely irresistible." All he said was : "Fellow countrymen, remember whence ye're sprung, and follow me to yonder saloon and thence to a glorious victory I" A POLITICIAN who was always in a quarrelsome mood, having very much annoyed a brother Senator, the latter suddenly turned upon him and asked "Why are you and a camel so much alike?" I give it up," was the reply. " Well," said the Senator, "it is because you both 'got your backs up' while young and have kept them so ever niace."

div.head: CATHERINE'S \MISTAKE,
div.p: CATHERINE'S \MISTAKE,
A SECRET FOR T.EARS.

CHAPTER LIV. IN SEARCH OF THE LOST OM A max December night, the rain beating against the casements, the wind howling fearfully among the great trees surrounding the house. Ingestre is alone, pacing his library up and down; George Ross no longer—master of Redfern no more. He listened to the wailing of the wind, and the loud splash of the rain upon the stone terrace; he listened, with but one thought in his mind. "She is abroad—braving this l" And then he ground his teeth, and beat his gent hollow chest. The loss of name and wealth that day was no loss to him compared with the loss of her. She was gone, had left him, and he dared not even seek her. In her eyes he was, a swindler, an impostor— she loved him no more. The tears fell down his burning cheeks—streamed from his aching eyes, and he wept like a woman. The being he most loved in the world was the one most injured by the great lie of his life. Fame, child, and fortune had been lost to her through his wrong doing. Seventeen long weary years of her youth had been passed as a wanderer, and little better than an outcast on the face-of the earth. And now the time had come that, through him and his second lie, she had gone forth onee more, a blighted and hope- less creature. The last look at her face told him her mind was on the verge of departing; that wherever she went there was little reason to guide her steps. And he thought, with horror too deep for words, of the dark night, the wild, pathless park, and the dark river; for the lake was a flowing river now, and the bridge from the village was scarcely fordable. And then that horror beset him, and became the prevailing idea of his mind—the river, the island, and something floating among the long reeds and tangled lily stems close by it. He could not sit nor stand, nor even stride the narrow room—the horror was se strong upon him. He rushed to the window and threw it wide open, and leaned out, only to gasp for breath, and stare into the dark night. The rain dashed on his face„ and the wind lifted his hair; but the storm and the utter darkness brought no consolation with it. It only seemed as if the night was ready to engulf any for- lorn waif within the compass of its gloom, and the cruel, wailing, drifting wind howling in triumph., over some treacherous act it had just been guilty of., Then while he stood there, all but paralysed with the horror of his thoughts, a cry, a screech rather, same drifting to his ears on a gust of wind. Another and another followed, more dismal than the last, and then the blast of wind was gone, careering far over the moors, leaving everything else still. A strange calmness fell upon him. He'closect the. window, and came back into the centre of' the room_ His face was deathly pale, and his eyes had a wild, iitartled expression; still that expression was not utterly senseless. He sat down for a moment leaning his' forehead in his hands, seeming, as it were, to collect and adjust his thoughts. Then he arose,. an& walked with a firm step out of the room. Everything was quiet outside, and he went on Into the hall, where he took down his cloak and hat, and put them on. Then he rang the servants' 'bell, and Domingo appeared in a moment; for, to tell the truth, the black had been lying in the shadow of a bronze at' the further end of the hall, watching the door of the: room which contained his master. Domingo, I want a lantern." And he, stood there patiently, staring at vacancy,. until the black returned with the lighted lantern.. Domingo looked piteously at the strangely cold, tin- passive face of his master. "Sere may I come too?" his livid, trembling lips. whispered. "'Norremain here; I don't want you," and Ingestra, started off: Domingo stood at the door, and watched him turn' Into a footpath across the park—watched him until the glimmering light was eclipsed by the intense dark- ness; and then, gently closing the door behind him, the faithful creature, bareheaded, went out into the. stormy night, too, and followed him closely. Ingestre went on and on, through mud, and marsh,. and mire. He went beneath those huge old chestnut.' trees Catherine spoke of long ago, then stood upon the' edge of thelake, and near to the boat-house before- mentioned He turned his light upon the water, and it gleamed in, a tiny ray upon its broad surface,. broken into miniature billows by the wind and rain. It was, only for a moment he remained thus; be• unlocked the door of the house, and entering its dark, slimy interior, proceeded to fasten his light in the prow' of' the boat. That was soon done, and then. with it powerful stroke of the oar, he shot her, out Into deep water. He pulledvzith long, sweeping strokes, with all the strength of his strong arms, through the dark, dan- gerous water, in the direction of the island. Itwas a. difficult-task, for it was a night of intense darkness, and' he bad no solitary point by which to steer his ' course. But, at last, the boat grounded, the oar I struck, and he lifted the lantern, and saw the great willows in a dark mass above him.

div.head: CHAPTER LV. MAXALL'S DOOM.
div.p: CHAPTER LV. MAXALL'S DOOM.

GIZOTOITT DTGESTRE iL-i-e-lreii-tl-1-13-1;;;t, as well as the . able, to, one of the swaying boughs of the willows,. and 'then, taking the light in his hand, he proceeded', to walk, round the island. Once he stood still, and shouted, with a force thai carried his cry far above the wildteating of the wind— " Catherine, Catherine!" Tbere,was ne reply. Be strained to catch,somer faint eeho to his call, but none came; and he went on, madly plunging through bush and bramble, mud aod water, ever crying— " Oho Catherine, Catherine !—lost—dad! Tbe light he held shed a faint and flickering mew on the shrubs and leafless trees about him, but it was useless. to aid him so far as careful search was required. Yet, feeble as it was, it served to,show sousething he had searcely come there to find: It has been before said that the water of thelake had risen, high above its usual level, and psrtially submerged a portion of the island. Here the long reeds, and tall rushes were matted thickly together under the water, and forased of themselves another island, divided from the patens one by a, flowing stream,

Among these reeds and grasss turned upwards to the sky, was a human face. Its deadly whiteness shone oat most horribly, amid the dark. meal of tangled stems and roots in which it lay. Iligestre saw the awful sight, and, with sr dismal yell, leaped the gulf dividing. hint from it, and alighted knee-deep in water and mud, close to the , spot near which it reposed, calmly staringar the dark sky; frT the eyes were wide, open, and the mouth filled with slime and water. Anil there he stood, or, rather waded, with his lantern turned full on that face. ',This is a relief," he Birthed. and looked again at the body at his feet, only partially out of the reach of the strong current. The face was not Catherine's, but ia was one ho knew as well. It was that of the boy whom he bad always supposed to be his brother's son, and the rightful heir of the property be held. It was the face of Maxall that now buy among the rushes and lily. stems, staring up at the dark, starless. sky. The face of a murderer, whom. God's punishment had over- taken at last. , Ingestre turned away, and left the body there. It ' was a corpse; what avail could areything living be to it now? So he argued; to appease the upbraiding cry of his heart at the inhumanity of the action. But, in fact, his dread of that loathsome face, that awful sight, drove him irresistibly away from it. To see the water dabbling with the hair—splashing over the white face—lifting the small body with heavy thuds. No! Alone with such a sight, in that wild spot. on that wild night, was more than he could endure and retain his senses. He piunged back through the sedgy gulf, anti rm.hed across the island to re-enter the boat. It was gone! The rope, decayed with weather, had snapped in two, and the boat had drifted or been blown far out of reach. He did not hesitate an instant ; but, flinging; the lantern away, his bat as well, plunged headlong inta the lake, and swam for his life. For his life? Yes, 1 he had not a thought of resigning it. He had not a I single idea of giving that guilty life up, stained, as it was, to its Maker. In all the horror of that day's exposures— in all its overwhelming shame, the man's better nature war true to itself, and the cry of his half-broken heart, his sorely bruised spirit WAS. "I will live to atone! Grant me life to repent! And, therefore, he struggled manfully with the dangerous tide, and swam as men do for their lives. He was preserved. He felt his feet touch the stony bottom, and then a fearful gust of wind drove him, and a mountain of water, safely on to the bank, where he clutched at the wet masses of grass and fern-stems he knew grew all along it. He stood upright at last, safely landed on the greenawasd of the Dark, and he hastened on to the

house, the memory of what he had left trhind causing his steps almost to fly. He entered bY the front door, for Cleland was standing there, with it wide apen, and the rain beating down on her unprp- teeted face. She uttered an exclamation of joy at the sight of her father. "At last! Oh, papal.! could not believe I should ever see you again. Parkins told me you had gone out. How wet! and no hat! Papa ?" She looked eagerly up into his face. It was calftg enough—nothing there to terrify her; and he smiled and kissed her as he said—
"The wind took my hat in crossing the park; We, shall find it to-morrow. How is Lina ? "

"She is asleep. We have seen nothing of Ingrant Ingestre, but a man left a note ten minutes ago foe you; he came from Lowraoor, and said it was most important. See, papa, I put it in the bosom of my' dress—here It is, but first you must change your wet clothes." •
He snatched it from her, tore it open, and: read "Mr. Ingestre's presence is required at the Mill souse, Lowmoor. A lady, seriously ill, is itMloll9 to see him."

This, then, was the end of it all; Catherine was ilr—dying. He had killed her; and now there was nothing to be done but ride those six miles vilth the best speed he could, and hoar the last wordir she should utter. The man of 'ungovernable passions was calm and collected now the worst of all had come upon him and the leaden despair at his heart brought him a:. least quiet. He gave orders for his fastest horse tc be saddled, and then sought out the baroness to ask her protection for his only possession, Cleland, in his. absence. "You area good-hearted woman, baroness. You leved George well, I know, and will be kind to poor Cle for his sake, if not for mine. If Ido not returr, make no inquiries after me, but take the best meant, to prove Ingram's rights,. and Lina's, too. But, oh! look after dc! love and be kind to her, and never let her suffer for my sins.' In all the wind and rain the poor girl stood holding the horse at the foot of the wide stone steps, and looking fearfully into the darkness through which her father was to pass: Be tried to escape parting with the only creature whose love he could call his own. But it was not to be. She put her arms round him, and he looked, tenderly down upon her pale, thin face. "My,darting! I have Ent bees a good parent to thee.* "Papa, you have loved me. What more could I

want?" "Not been a good father to thee, my child— wronged thee frightfully. But, ola t I meant not to d 3 it! What fortune wilt thou have now, Cle, wh am gone? None. Thank Heaven, my boy is dead! spared this I Forgive merchild ! forgive me before I go!" " Go! go where?" she cried: "Father, go where?' She clung to him, and would not let hi in mount. "Go where? she screamed, for the high wind almost drowned the voices. He tore her hands from the reins* kissed her pig' sionately, then mounted and dashed away. Above the wind he heard that shrill scresm repeated, "Father! go where ?" and, as he rode. every gust seemed to bring the echo to his ear.

div.p: OPENING OF PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—Ttraspea.

The fifth session of the twefth Parliament of the Queen, and of the twenty-fourth Parliament of the United King- dom of Great Britain and Ireland, was opened on Tues- day by Royal Commission. Long before the hour ap- pointed for the opening ceremony, visitors began to take their places in the House of Lords, and the attendance of . ladies was unprecedentedly numerous, more than one hundred being seated in the body of the House. The wleole of the four rows of back benches on the Opposi- tion side were appropriated to them, an fully occupied; and among the spectators who filled the Strangers' Gal_ iery there were many more ladies than gentlemen. There evere also some few ladies in the side galleries. Only About a dozen peers were present, and they were all seated on the Ministerial side of the House. Amongst , them were the Archbishop of Canterbury, the Bishop of 1 Bangor, the Duke of Bedford, Lord Denman, Lord Bram- well, Lord Munaird, and Lord Headley. The Lord Chancellor, in his full robes, and attended tri his mace bearer and purse bearer, entered at two ()clock from the bar, and passed through the House to the Prince's-chamber, from whence he shortly after- wards reterned, accompanied by the Earl of Mount- Edgcumbe, the Earl of Limerick, Lord Cross and Lord Knutsford, all. as Reval Commissioners, wearing their full peers' robes of scarlet and ermine. The Commissioners having taken their seats upon a bench placed in front of the Throne, Admiral Sir James Drummond, the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, received the directions of the Lord Chancellor to sum-, mon the Commons. After a short interval, the Speaker, attended by Sir James Di ummend on his right, and the Sergeant-at- Anns on his left, appeared at the bar, followed by °con- siderable numner of members of the Lower House, amongst whom the most ccnspicuously placed were the Attorney-General, Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, Mr. Demo Collings, Mr. Sydney Gedge, Mr. Buchanan, Mr. J. Shiress Will, Mr. Pickton, Sir R. Temple, Mr. R. G. Webster, Sir W. Foster, and Mr. .1. Ellis. The Lord Chancellor announced, in the usual :corm, that her Majesty, not thinking fit to be present in person nn that occasion, had directed a commission under the eeteat seal to be issued for the opening of Parliament. The Reading Clerk, the Hon. Slinggby BetheK, then readthe commission, after which The Lord Chancellor said—My Lords and Gentlemen --lire are commanded to deliver to you her Majesty's 'Speech in her Majesty's own words. He then proceed 'to read. THE QUEEN'S SF'EECH. :MY LORDS AND GENTLEBLES,— My relations with other Powers continue to be of a , 'friendly character. An armed force under a Portuguese officer was despatched during the autumn from the; , colony of Mozambique into territory where British' • tsettlements had been formed, and where there are native 'tribes who have been taken under my •pretection. A t 'collision, attended with bloodshed, took place, and acts , 'were committed inconsistent with the respect due to the 'flag of this country. The Portuguese Government have s- 'new at my request promised to withdraw their military 'f• orces from the territory in,question. A Conference of the Powers interested in the supgres- fe• Mon of the slave trade has 'been convoked at Brusselsiby •▪ the King of the Belgians. I earnestly hope that • the results of its deliberations will advancathe great case for which it is assembled. ie A Commercial Garreention has been concluded with t, the Khedive of Egypt, and a provisional arrangement r, for the adjustment of pressing`fiscil questions has been et made with the Government of Bulgaria. s Papers on all these questions will be presented to .you. The Convention concluded by metwith the Emperor of Germany and the Republic Of the ,United States *with respect to the government of Samoa will be laid before You, together with the protocols of the Conference, as also a treaty which has been concluded with the United • States for amending the law of extradition between the two countries. The latter instrument still awaits ' the ratification of the Senate. The disordered condition of Swaziland having tendered it necessary to make provision for the better government ef that territory, the independence Of which was recog- nised by the Convention of London, I have, acting in Conjunction with the President 'of the South African , Republic, sent a Commiesionerto learn the views of the Swazis and of the white settlers. I shall await with lively interest the result of the Con- ference now being held to discusirtheimportantquestion Of the Federation of the Australian Colonies. Any well- considered measure which, by bringing these great colonies into closer union, will increase their welfare and strength will receive my favourable consideration. GENTLEMEN OF THE HOUSE OF 'COMMONS,— The estimates of the year for defraying theesost of the government of the country will be laid before you. They have been drawn with a due -regard to economy and to the necessities of the public service. MY Loans AND GENTLEMEN, The continued improvement 'lathe state of Ireland and the further diminution in theamount of agrarian crime have made it possible very largely to restrict-the area in which it is necessary to deal with certain offences by summary process. Proposals for increasing under due financial preceution the number of occupying owners, for extending to Ireland the principles of local self- eovernnsent which have ~heady been adopted in England and Scotland, so far as they are applicable to that country, and for improving the material well-being of the population in the poorer districts will be submitted to you. A bill for facilitating and 'cheapening the transfer of land in England will be again presented to yeti. Provisions will be submitted to you for diminishing . the difficulty and cost which at present attentlthe pas- sage of private legislation required for Scotland. A bill for improving the procedure by which tithe is -Ilciw levied and for facilitating its redemption will be laid before you. I have appointed a Commission to report 'upon the • best means of improving the economic conditions which • a...lfeet the inhabitants of some parts of the 'Western Highlands and islands of Scotland. Your attention will be invited again to a bill for ascer- taining the liability of employers in case of accidents, and to a measure for improving the procedure in Winding up insolvent companies under the Limited Liability Acts, There will be laid before you bills for a consolidation and amendment of the laws with respect to public health in the metropolis and to the dwellings of the Working classes, and also a bill for the better 'regulation Of Savings Banks and Friendly Societies. • Your attention will be directed to the state of the entninodation now provided in camps and barracks, and you will be asked to make better provision for the distribution as well as for the health and comfort of my troops. I commend you earnestly in the discharge of your high responsibility to the care and guidance of Almighty Goo. Immediately after the reading of the Speech, the Speaker and members of the House of Commons with- drew from the bar, the Lord Commissioners retired, and the ceremony was thus brought to a close at a quarter Past two o'clock. When,, at a quarter past four o'clock, the Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack, there was a full house, and most of the seats in the side galleries Were occupied by peeresses. The leaders on both sides Were in their places and the Prince of Wales was in his etostomary seat on the cross benches Both the mover and seconder of the Address wore military uniform. The )4arquis of Salisbury, on entering the holqie, wasgreeted With Ministerial cheers.—The Lord Chancellor read the , Queen's Speech. THE ADDRESS. Lord DE RAMSEY having moved and the Earl of STRAD- man seconded the Address in reply to the Speech, Lord • e kativitta criticised the late meeting of Parliament as ' ueing injudicious in the present state of public business, L'ad also animadverted on the assumption by Lord Sails- 'an? of two such arduous offices as those of Prime Min- ter and Foreign Secretary. Lord Granville also criti- . daed the tone of Lord Salisbury's despatches to the Portu- ' gliese Government, and afterwards referred to the diffi- •Lllties of satisfactorily dealing with the tithes question. bile admitting an improvement in the state of Ireland, tle did not believe it was attributable to the manner in rich the present Government had administered the law. rd SALISBURY, in reply, defended the arrangement lender which he combines the ofAces of Prime Minister 4174 Foreign Secre ary, repeated the opinions he has e/teressed at Newport and Nottingham in favour of the Principle of free education, and with reference to Portu- gal dwelt on the absolute necessity of acting promptly ri.d firmly. Touching on Ireland, Lord SALISBURY main- that the system of government pursued had en,,Tninished the prevalence of crime. The Address was .7.,sseed to, and the Earl of Morley was reappointed , e ilairman of Committees. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. v.ln the House of Commons the bustle of preparation for ele fast day of the new session commenced almost with 'eaebrealr. The cleaners were at work in the House Ziosttly after six, but they had hardly completed their within the Chamber itself when the gentlemen for • m they were putting things n order themselves __• Innaenced t ) enter upon the scene. The first to arrive .7aB Mr. Macartney, who presented himself at the Cwguylarly early hour of five minutes past nine. He, te was not alone in his anxiety to be amongst ble nSt to choose a place for the opening night. Mr. 0,,,f7n-Hartland shared it with him, and came down to atre a seat some five minutes later. He was followed ten min was rites past nine by Mr. Picton, who in turn the e..rwed by Mr. Swift this gentleman having seinction of being the first Irish member to put in :11..aPpearance. At 10,20 Sir John Colomb came in, and 10.45 Sir Felward Ihrkbeck and Mr. Leake—the earli- M._arricaval fr:mn the County Palatine. Shortly afterwards thee _rule a crowd of members, numbering amongst Sir W. Lawson, Professor Stuart, Mr. mgs, Mr. Caine, Mr. Addison, and Mr. F. S. By hulidred a quarter to two o'clock there were over a upon e e ats—mostly with the brilliance of newness there _Ll'', 111—brim uppermost on the benches, placed m th„ and ticketed by their owners to secure places for ' The flint member of the Government to
I

appear was the Solicitor-General, although his colleague the Attorney-General had been noticed in the lobby some time before. Two subordinate members of the Govern- ment—namely, Mr. Stuart-Wortley and Sir H. Maxwell —also attended in the Chamber, hut save by these the Ministry had no one to represent them in the ceremonies forming a prelude to the coming of Black Rod. The Speaker, attended by his chaplain and the Ser- geant-at-ilrins bearing, the mace, entered the House just before two O'clockoviten the galleries were cleared.`After prayers the reporters and the public were readmitted. The usual greetings were being exchanged between the Speaker and members when the ceremony was inter- rupted by the advent of the message from the House of Lords. Members were filing past the Speaker—who was seated in the chair usually occupied by the Clerk to the House—and were shaking hands with the right hon. gentleman in turn, and there were still some 50 or 60 to I go by, when the doors were closed with a clang and Black Rod's knock was heard at the portal. The doors were opened, the House of Lords' functionary was an- nounced, members fell back huvriedly on either side, the Speaker took the chair, and Black _Rod entered, walked with stately stride to the table, and delivered his message requesting the attendance of the Speaker and the Commons to the bar of the House of Lords to hear the Royal Com Mission opening Parliament and the ' Queen's Speech read. The Speaker obeyed the summons, with the majority of the members present. He was absent about a quarter of an hour, and on his return he I walked through the House—the mace being left upen the table—entering by the font door and retiring by the door at the beck of the chair, the sitting being ens- ' pended until dour o'clock. NEW MEMBERS. _ _

The formal resolutions---s-v-hiCii—open all Sessions having been recited and agreed to, the Speaker called upon members 'desirous of taking their 'seats to come to the table. The first in the long procession was Captain Verney, who during the recess has won a seat for Liberalism in North Bucks, and now received a hearty diner frorp Liberals. Next came Mr. Long, who succeeded Mr. Firth in Dundee; after. Mr. Keay, newly-elected for Elgin and Nairn; then Mr. Chaplin, brought up by Sir M. Hicks Seach and Mr. Stanhope, and visibly blushing as his party cheered him, and hon. gentlemen on the opposite bendhes good- humouredly smiled. Almost simultaneously &procession of Ministers arrived. First was Mr. Smith„ followed by Mr. Goschen, Lord George Hamilton, the Solicitor- General. Mr. Riimhie, and Baron de Worms. Mr. Morton, who won a seat in Peterborough, was loudly cheered by the LToerals, the Conservatives taking up the cheers when Mr. Loder, who held a Ministerial seat at Brighton, was escorted to the table by his chief, Mr. Ritchie. The louder and longer cheering was necessarily with the Liberals, since they hailed the victors in four seats, two of them wrested from the enemy, whilst the 'triumph on the Conservative side was limited to not losing three other seats. THE FORGED LETTERS.—BREAViI OF PRIVILEGE. It was ten minutes to six when Sir William Harcourt rose, his appearance at the table being hailed with a hearty cheer from the Opposition benches. Sir William Harcourt spoke for something over half an hour in .v tone and style the moderation .iff which received. acknowledgment from Sir John Gorst when he came to reply. One rare lapse into strong language happened when he denounced the, forged letter as a foal and felonious assault on &member et the House. He pointed out that it had been procured and held in hand or publication on the morning of the 18th of April, 186.7, preceding by a few hours the division on the second reading of the Coercion Act. It was impossible to eon- , ceive a grosser and more -palpable breach of the privileges of the House than the publication of the letter and comments by which it was accompanied.' Ile invited members on both sides to Join in giving voioeto an authoritative denunciation ef the arts of political forgery. He was sorry that the task of moving the resolution he had in charge had not been undertaken by the responsible Leader of the House. Referring to the Act of Union and the pledge then given the.; Irish members should be placed on the same footing in the; House of Commons as members for British constituencies, he asked what course would have been taken supposing on the morning of a vote of confidence in the Govern- ment a charge involving the private character of Mr. Smith had appeared in "The Times," or that that journal had accused the Chancellor of the Exchequer of malversa- tion of public funds ? What measure would they deal to the Irish members who sit amongst them when they' were attacked in similar circumstances ? "I have," Sir William said, amid loud cheers, "spoken of the promise of the Union. We shall see to-night what is the performance." He concluded by moving a resolution declaring the forged letter to be a false and scandalous libel and& breach of the privileges of the House. Sir John Gorst, on rising, was greeted with a cordial', cheer, token of his general popularity in the House, and acknowledgment of the honour done to him during the recess by his admission to the rank of Privy Councillor. But, as Mr. Gladstone took occasion_to_ observe, this

welcoming cheer was not sustained. Sir John had e. bad case, and dealt with it in a somewhat cynical manner. There were, he said, three reasons why the resolution should not be agreed to. The first was that there was no precedent for a question of privilege being raised after so long an interval from the alleged offence. The econd was that the case being still sub udice, the report of the Commissioners not yet being publis'hed, it was too soon. At this stage of the argument the interposition of a stranger arrested the attention of the still crowded House. A mouse, apparently sharing the bewilderment of the audience, and desiring to draw nearer to the orator, darted across the bar and made straight in the direction of Sir John Gorst. A shout of surprise arrested its progress, and, doubling, it made for the deorway,, cannoning against a stalwart member for a home county who stood by the cross benches. The hon. member, unprepared for the manoeuvre, displayed an agitation that greatly amused the House. " 'rhe Times" libel, breach of privilege, the resolution, and Sir John Gorst's argument were all forgotten. Members stood up in their places eagerly watching the mouse and the scared mem- ber; Sir John, not grasping the situation, staring round in bewilderment. The mouse, frightened by the gyrat- ing member, again doubled, and finally disappeared in the neighbourhood of the cross benches. When order was restored Sir John Great stated his third reason against the resolution, which was that it did not refer to a case in which it would redound to the honour and dignity of the House to invoke privilege. He concluded by moving an amendment declaring that the House de- clined to treat as a breach of privilege the publication of the forged letters and the comments thereon. The dinner hour was now approaching, and when Mr. Robert Reid rose members hurried off to dress. Mr. Reid spoke for only a quarter of an hour, and when he sat down no one seemed inclined to waste a speech on ; the almost empty benches. In this dilemma Mr. Glad-1 stone interposed. Members had, however, widely dis- persed, and the vigorous speech in which Mr. Gladstone supported the resolution had an unusually small audience. To the shifting argument of the Under-Secretary for India as to the soonness or the lateness of the motion, Mr. Gladstone opposed the fact that Tuesday was the earliest moment since the offence was committed at which it was possible to submit a motion to the House. .

When Mr. Gladstone sat down desolation fell upon the House, and Mr. Balfour's interposition did not prevent the falling away. Mr. Parnell rose at twenty minutes past eleven, and the House suddenly filled, members in the lobby being called in by the wild cheer with which the Irish members hailed their chief. Mr. Parnell was brief, but unusually emphatic and imppressive, hon. members opposite sitting mute under the blows delivered with telling effect. Mr. Parnell's last reproach was a declaration that by the course taken by the Government they still led the public and the world to believe that a doubt lingered around the genuineness of the letters which "The Times" had attributed to him. He there- , fore moved to add the word "forged" as an adjective ' preceding the word "letters" in Sir John Gorst's amendment. MI. Smith promptly accepted this sugges- tion, taking the opportunity to express on behalf of himself, his colleagues, and his party his detestation of the means by which the attack was fastened on Mr. Parnell, and his satisfaction at his absolute freedom from the imputation. Just on the stroke olgwelve the House divided, the motion being negativedld 260 votes against 212, thus reducing the Ministerial majority to 48, a significant fact much cheered from the opposition Benches. Mr. Smtxtr intimated that the debate on the Address would be taken at 12 o'clock on Wednesday, and would be suspended about 3.30, in order to allow Bills to be brought in. The House adjourned at five minutes past twelve. The division on the Privilege debate was conducted on strict party lines. The Dissentient Liberals voting with the Government were :—Mr Chamberlain, Mr. Biddulph, Mr. T. W. Russell, Mr. J. More, Colonel Cornwallis West, Mr. F. W. McLean, Hon. A. Elliot, Sir H. Havelock Allan, Mr. Jesse Collings, Mr. Heneag,e, Mr. Caldwell, and Mr. It. Chamberlain. .
HOUSE OF COMMONS, WEDNESDAY.
The Speaker took the chair at a quarter-past twelve.

- THE LABOUR CONFERENCE AT BERNH. Mr. BAUMANN.—I beg to ask the Under Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs whether, in consequence of the postponement of the Labour Conference at Berne, fresh invitations have been issued by the Swiss Government to the European Powers, and, if so, whether he will state what answer England returned ? Sir J. FERCIIISSON.—Yes, sir; a fresh invitation has been received, but it has not yet been replied to. Mr. Ga./aux.—May I ask the right hon, gentleman if he can inform the House whether it is contemplated to furnish the British delegates with powers to discuss any question? Sir J. FERGIISSON.—The invitation has been received recently—only within, I think, the last day or two—and I cannot say what will be done until it has been con- sidered by her Majesty's Government.

div.head: TRH EXCITEMENT IN PORTUGAL.
div.p: TRH EXCITEMENT IN PORTUGAL.

Mr. CREMER.—i beg to ask the Under Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs whether his attention has been called to the numerous statements which have appeared in the press concerning the excited state of. public opinibn in Portugal, and the hostility displayed towards British subjects resident there.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 15, 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 15, 1890.

Sir. J. Fanoussiox.--Her Majesty's Government are aware that popular feeling in Portugal has been greatly disturbed by the late difference between the Govern- ments of the two countries. I believe the facts as they will appear in the papers presented to Parliament, on Wednesday. will largely dispel the misapprehension from which that feeling arose. The relations between the two Governments are friendly. The Portuguese Government have suggested the referenceof the questions in dispute to arbitration, but her Maje4y'B Government consider the circumstances inapplicable to that principle. (Minikterial cheers.) DEBATE ON THE ADDRFAR, The Address in reply to the Queen's Speeett was ' moved by Mr. T. B. ROYDEN, and seconded by Lord I BROOKE. Mr. GworroNE said there was no disposition on the part of those on his side the House to call in ques- tion the administration of foreign affairs. He agreed that there was cause for action in the Portuguese affair, and thought that it was better that that action should be prompt, though he took exception to the tone adopted by the Foreign Minister. The right hon. gentleman ex- pressed a hope that the Government would put the country in possession of the facts in regard to matters in Armenia and Crete, and glanced ac the subjects omitted from the Speech, among which he noticed assisted educa- tion and the Sugarronveztion. Mr. Swan defended the attitude of her Majesty's Government towards Portugal, and said they believed that the Portuguese Government, recognising the justice of the claims we had made, would come shortly to an understanding that would render any further difficulties unnecessary. As to the question of assisted education, the Government were not in a posi- tion to appropriate to it this sessionthe large amount of time which it wonl&require ; and in regard to the Sugar Convention, there did not yet exist that agreement among the powers which was necessary for immediate legislation. The debate was adjoarned on the motion of Mr. HOWORTH, and a large number of private bills having been read, the House rose at five 'o'clock. MESE OF LORDS.—Tuensrar.
