div.head: I THE LATE MR. McMINNIES.
div.p: I THE LATE MR. McMINNIES.
FUNERAL SERNION.

On Sunday evening the Rev. John Yonge, pastor of Wycliffe Congregational Church, Bewsey-st., made eloquent allusion to the death of Mr. McHinnies, his remarks being listened to with great attention by a large congregation. In consequence of the chapel having been closed for renovation, the service was held in Wycliffe Hall. Mr. Yonge took as his text the words—y As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all " (Galatians, vi.). After speakirg of the text in its general application, Mr. Yonge continued: I think it will be manifest why I have selected this text for this occasion. I have done so because it seems to set so clearly forth the principle characteristic, and per- haps the moat successful and worthy lesson of Mr. McMinnies' life, most certainly of that portion of it which has come under my own observation. It was not my privilege to known him before I knew Wycliffe. But immediately upon my settlement here I was introduced to him, and our relations have been cordial and even intimate wail the end. In what I shall say now, I shall mainly speak of him as I have known him. Many words of admiration and affection have already been spoken concerning him, some by men who have known him from the beginning of his more public life in this town. It is. of course, customary, and conventional, to speak only in language of respect of the recently departed, and so it might be supposed that this general lan- guage of admiration was largely so prompted. Such an idea, however, in this case, would be untrue. Without claiming for our friend greater virtue than he possessed, without blindness to defects in his character, which may have made themselves apparent, I feel it a privilege and an honour to speak of him here and now as a man of great worth, of high intelligence, and deeply sym- pathetic nature, and rare unselfishness. All that others have said a him already in these respects is more than justified by my own knowledge of the facts of his career and character. There was much in him that was exemplary. How well it speaks for his intelligence and integrity, and for his wise use of talent and opportunity, that he should have risen as he had from a humble beginning to become a leader of men in the community, and fora time their representative in the senate of the nation ! When our friend, as a youth, was apprenticed at a cotton mill in Lancaster, it never entered his head that he would one day have a seat in the House of Commons. Nor, probably, did he then imagine that he would be able to make his way in commerce and society with such conspicuous success. But it is obvious that from the beginning he must have made up his mind to be industrious and reliable; he must have resolved to devote his best attention to his work and business, with the purpose of doing the best he could. How many young fellows there are who never seem to regard their work or busi- ness in that fashion. I confess that there appears to be in a large number of instances a tremendous lack of aspiration and inspiration. Youths and young men seem content to take things very easy, and to imagine if their way in life does not open of its own accord no effort of their own can make it open. If Mr. McMinnies had looked at life like that, you and I would never have known him, and never been interested in speaking of him to-night. Why will not some of you take heart from his example, and go in for making your way? Because you are in a humble rank to-day, my friend, is no reason why you should continue there until your dying day. Every youth should aspire and labour to rise. It may entail long endeavour, and many a self- denial, and resolute discipline, much work and little play. You may encounter many a rebuff, many a dis- appointment and defeat, but if you will use brain, and muscle, and will, you will achieve. Put your heart as well as your head into your work, and by God's blessing you may make your life a good and true success. Our friend was from his youth not only industrious in his daily work, but he was also diligent in informing his min-d. He did not have the benefit of what is called a good education. He was a British School boy at Lancas- ter, and gained what learningsuch a school in those days could give. Every boy, however, who sits in this build- ing day by day, under the teaching staff of our day school, receives an education unspeakably in advance of any that our friend would receive. But he set himself to reading and study, thereby forming literary habits and tastes which in later days he turned to many useful purposes, and which in the closing years of his life brought him continual solace and refreshment. ' It might, perhaps, have tended to his greater physical health and vigour throughout his life had he been able in youth to engage in athletic games, as now a-days se many of our young men are accustomed to. But in that case perhaps he would have done as so many of them are doing to-day, have sacrificed his mental improvement to his muscular development. Therein he would have impaired his social usefulness, and robbed his life's evening of the pleasant and profit- able companionship of books. If a youth has any ambition to rise, he must cultivate mind as much as body, and he must devote leisure hours to something better than mere gossip and amusement. Now, I think that Mr. McMinnies must, very early in his career, have aspired to be very useful to his fellowmen. I think so, because that, most assuredly,was the desire of the latter years of his life. And men do not newly develop any such desire as that in later days. A man who has lived for him- self until he is middle-aged, rarely over-comes the habit of selfishness. But, inasmuch as upwards of forty years ago our friend began to try and serve his fellow-towns- men; it is clear that his sympathies early led him to seize any "opportunity to do good unto all." No doubt there are some men who seek conspicuous position in a community for the mere love of prominence, and because they think they can coin advantage for themselves out of such prominent position. So far, however, as my reading of his character goes, I cannot imagine our friend to have been ever governed by any such motives. lie thought that the condition of this any was capable of improve- ment and development. Therefore he laboured to bring such results about. "As he had opportunity "—the opportunity of talent, leisure, and occasion—he sought

"to do good "to this town, by promoting its better government as a municipality, by aiding in its educa- tional development, and by according unstinted help to all its varied philanthropies. Now, I say emphati- cally that in all this he has left behind him a worthy , example. There are many young men here to-night, who should derive stimulus from his conduct to resolve upon,. and to carry out, a career of social use- fulness in this town The Council Chamber of a town, the guidance and control of a political party, ought to be in the possession of the best ;and most intelligent, and most upright men ; of men who are actuated by unselfish and patriotic motives; of men who will do right because itis right, and who will elevate the general tone of public and commercial life. I will go so far as to say that these positions are worthy of the earnest services of avowedly Christian men ; only, they must take their Christian principle with them into their conspicuous positions, and give it there unmistakable display. It needs to be clearly understood that a Christian man, who devotes time and talent to caring for the physical and social conditions of a community,is pur- suing a Christian ministry as truly as he may be doing who is giving his life to preaching the gospel. We are learning in these days that social needs, social conditions, present strong claims on Christian service. The Arch- bishop of Canterbury has sounded a true note in his recently published visitation addressfs, when he says that the condition of society is the test of the churches. I must hasten on. This is not the time to refer to the political life of our friend, save to say that his political principles he adopted and advocated with great intelligence, and cherished them as the profound convictions of his conscience. He believed intensely in the rightness of Liberalism, and expended thought, time, money, and toil in its promo- tion. He equally disbelieved in the rightness of the opposite view, and combated it with unfaltering fidel- ity. But so far as my knowledge of him extends, his political controversy was never inspired by a bitter spirit; he did not himself indulge in malicious and wounding sarcasm; and he deprecated the use of such speech by others. Hence it is that even his political opponents vie with his political friends in their langu- age of commendation of his life, and regret at his death, and that they mingled so freely in the large concourse around his grave. How well it would be if all political controversy could be purged of personal animosity, and if argument could be rescued from the company of satire and invective! No good purpose in this world was ever served by the use of hard words, or by the call- ing of bad names. It is possible to be honest without being offensive, and to repudiate principles without blackening persons. There ought, in my opinion, to be a reform introduced into political controversy. It is said that as a naticn, Engiand is losing its courtesy and good manners. Certainly there is not unfrequently a lamentable lack of good behaviouron political platforms, and in political conflict statements are made, charges are laid, attacksare directed against persons, which are unscrupulous, unfounded, and. untrue. With some it seems the merest trifle to utter or circulate a falsehood. All this needs reforming ; and no one felt this more than our late friend. He has more than once spoken to me as occasion afforded, of the unwisdom of unguarded public speech, of political lampooning, of caricature, of invective: and of his wish that political life could be delivered from such extravagances. Ever was our friend on the popular side. Not because he courted popularity, but because he loved the people. Every movement for the last half century in furtherance of civil or religious liberty had his sympathy. Time pre- vents even a cursory allusion to the great achievements of that period in which he sympathized, and to which, to greater or smaller extent, he helped. I may, how- ever, be allowed a single reference, because it is due to his memory. and is occasioned by a statement that has been published since his death. It has been said by the writer of an article in a local paper that Mr. McMinnies was out of sympathy with the movement for Irish Home Rule, and that that was the main and real reason of his declining to seek re-election in 1885. The man who wrote that did not know Mr. McMinnies, and did not know the truth. He wrote what he may have wished, but he wrote what he did not know. I speak what I know, when I say that the state- ment thus made is untrue ; and that no more ardent friend to Ireland, or to the cause of Home Rule lives to-day than he whom we laid in his tomb last Tuesday. Mr. MeMinnies was a staunch Nonconformist. He held firm to dissent, although some who starter.' at his side, left Nonconformity and sought refuge in the Establishment. This fact is to his honour. Possibly it might have been, in some sort, to his social advantage if he could have waived his Nonconformist principles. He did not pass through his life without attempts being made to alter both his doctrinal views and his ecclesias- tical relations. But he resisted every endeavour to brine him into sympathy and adhesion to either an established or a priestly religion. Yet, he was a willing helper even of churches and sects with which he had but little intel- lectual agreement. The Vicar of this parish has already made public acknowledgment of frequent kindly help. And I have no doubt that even the Catholic clergy could tell of gifts for their charitable funds. " As he had opportunity, he did good unto all " ; but, taking into view for a moment the remainder of the verse, he did good especially to "the household of faith" with which from childhood he had been identified. Here at Wycliffe, nearly all our institutions for a long number of years have been largely indebted to his generous help. When the church was built In 1872 he contributed to- wards the erection, and it was the rarest thing possible for him to decline to give to any object about this place. ' Nor was it in Warrington alone that he helped the Con- ' gregational body. In the village of Leyland, near Preston, near his Farrington mills, a handsome Congre- gational church now stands, which some 12 years ago he was mainly instrumental in building, and the building debt of which, either by begging or giving, he com- pletely removed. His religious views were broad and catholic. Willingly recognising the good in all creeds and churches, he held staunchly to Con- gregationalism because he believed it to present the broadest and freest platform of Christian belief and activity that can be found. Our friend never made what would have enriched his character still more, and increased his influence for good, and been a comfort to his heart—he never made what is called a religious profession. He used to speak tome sometimes of regard- ing a thing" from the standpoint of a worldly man," meaning that he considered that to be his own position. I think, however, that we should most piteously err if we took him at his own valuation, or if we at all concluded that because he made no so-called profession .of religion there was not in his heart, and largely animating his life, especially in his latter years,a true and real religiousness. I, at any rate, have occasion to believe in his appreciation of religious faith and comfort, and I know that about nothing was he more deeply interested than about the prosperity and spiritual usefulness of this Church. He

possessed considerable Biblical knowledge, and he had his own favourite Scriptures.and favourite hymns, about which he would sometimes speak. We have sung one of these hymns (Eternal Light) in this service. Among his favourite Scriptures were the " l'ara.ble of the Prodigal Son," and "The Sermon on the Mount :" the former of which he could never hear or read without deepest emotion as conveying to him a full and melting revelation of the Fatherhood of God. As for the spirit of the man, that was his charm. As one has said who for years has had intimate opportunity of knowing—" he never thought of himself. Be was happiest when doing, or getting, or giving, for the good or pleasure of others. He would often go out of his way to help. He had a heart to sympathise with all; sometimes encountering the imposition that is the fate of notorious kindness; but more often shedding wonderful benediction upon needy hearts and homes. He did not do good ostentatiously; but "did good by stealth, and blushed to find it fame." There are many who will have to thank God for Mr. McMinnies to their dying day, many who will miss a welcome sympathy and a generous friend now he has gone. A kinder, more tender hearted, quickly sym- pathetic, generous, and helpful man, it has never been my lot to know. It was impossible to know him without learning to esteem and love. He has gone to his rest ; adding one more to a large company of departed War- rington leaders in the last 10 years. Without any in- vidious comparison, deep as the regret may have been which was occasioned by their deaths, no member of this community has received so large a tribute of esteem as has our friend: and no loss that the town has suffered has been so widely felt as his. May young Warrington men learn to copy and follow all that was good and unselfish in our friend's character and life. Avoiding his defects, emulate his virtues. Strengthen your own characters increase your own influence and power by manly and loyal following of Jesus Christ. Lay yourselves out to be useful. As you have, or can find, or can make opportunity, do good unto all. That is the happy life. That surely is the life that leads on, and opens out, by God's mercy, into Heaven itself. MID-GLIMORGA.N ELECTION.

The Mid-Glamorgan Conservative Association at ai "Urgent " meeting on Wednesday, rselected Mr. Morti- mer, barrister, of London, and of the Welsh circuit, to contest, the vacant seat. Mr. S. T. Evans, of Neath, the Liberal candidate, has commenced his campaign, and met with a most encouraging reception.

div.head: A. ROYALIST SENT TO PRISON.
div.p: A. ROYALIST SENT TO PRISON.

The Due d'Orleans was brought before the Correctional Tribunal on Wednesday. He pleaded guilty to an infrac- tion of the banishment law, but asked if it were a crime to love his country and to seek to serve her. The :Court passed sentence of imprisonment for two years. A remarkable display of Royalist feeling took place in the courtroom and the streets adjacent.

SERIOUS COLLISION IN THE MERSEY. Early, on Thursday morning, the Swedish steamer Ilermod, while coming out of one of the Liverpool docks, outward bound for Gothenburg, was carried by a strong tide across the river, and came into violent col- lision with the barque Ebenezer, lying at anchor, out. ward bound for Buenos Ayres with coal. The barque was so seriously damaged that it sank in a few minutes before the crew could lower the boat. A steamer, how- ever, brought to anchor close by, and the boats were lowered, by which the crovr of the barque were saved.
INCREASED PAY FOR CIVIL SERVANTS.

The eagerly looked for Treasury minute regulating the future position of the lower division clerks of the ' Civil Service reached the heads of department on Mon- day morning. It provides that the salaries of the lower division clerks shall proceed without interruption to £250 per annum by annual increment of £7 10s., and thence on certificate of merit being obtained from the head of the department to a maximum of £350 by an- nual increment of £lO. This will apply uniformly to every department in the service, and it is expected that a further minute, dealing with superannuation and with the position of the higher division clerks, will be circu- lated shortly after the opening of Parliament.

div.head: WELCOME 10 MR. O'BRIEN.
div.p: A WELCOME 10 MR. O'BRIEN.

Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., was present on Wednesday night at a meeting of London Liberals and Radicals, held to welcome him on his resumption of Parliamentary duties after his imprisonment. Between four and five thousand people attended. Replying to an address, Mr. O'Brien said the people of England were beginning to understand and detest Mr. Balfour's policy. During the past four years Tories and renegade Liberals had been endeavouring to exasperate the Itish people against England by coercion and to prejudice Englishmen against Ireland by calumny and forgery, but they had failed. The Irish party had come out of coercion and subsidised defamation unscathed and unconquered.

div.head: SQUABBLING OVER THE DEAD.
div.p: SQUABBLING OVER THE DEAD.

At the meeting of the Board of Guardians on Wednesday, Mr. Harbourne, relieving officer, reported with regard to the burial of a child belong- ing to destitute parents which had died at the borough fever hospital. Dr. Gornall, the medical superintendent at the hospital, had called attention to the case, and Mr. Harbourne had seen to the burial, but he wished for definite instruction from the Guardians as to the way he was to deal with similar cases in the future.—The ASSISTANT CLEnx, having referred to the law on the subject, said it was optional for the Guardians to bury these bodies from the hospital. So long as the body was at the hospital it was the duty uf the hospital authorities to deal with it. If it weie removed to the mortuary, the Guardians would have to deal with it, but it could only be removed there by order of a magistrate, and he did not think the medical man in charge of the hospital, although a magistrate as Dr. Gornall was, should order the body to be taken to the mortuary. Dr. Gornall had, however, told him that he should order every such case to the mortuary in the future, but he (the Assistant Clerk) did not think he had any right to do that either as a medical practitioner or as a magistrate.—Mr. Hnerow ' said that, upon a person dying in a properly constituted hospital, it was for the hospital authorities to deal with , the body except upon the order of a magistrate.—The CHAIRMAN said that when the body got to the mortuary it was the duty of the Union to bury it.—The ASSISTANT CLERK: There is this to be said, we can do it cheaper than the hospital authorities.—The CHAIRMAN thought the most desirable and expeditious way, was for the Union to bury the body from the hospital as they would have to do it if it were sent to the mortuary.— Mr. OWEN moved, however, that they do not bury the bodies except from the mertuary.—Mr. Elneron seconded the proposal, which was carried.

div.head: CREWE MURDER.
div.p: THE CREWE MURDER.
THE HATCHET FOUND.

After a search of nearly a fortnight, the head of the hatchet which is supposed to have been the weapon with which the murdered man Mr. Davies, was hacked on Saturday fortnight, has been found. On Saturday morn- ing Inspector Oldham and Detective Inspector Free- borough were searching in the neighbourhood of the scene of the murder for the axe, and at last found it buried in he soft soil. Detective Freeboreugh was the first to unearth the handle of the hatchet, a week ago, but not knowing that the hatchet had a stale of the peculiar shape of the piece of stick he threw it back into the hedge bottom. When he became aware of what it was it had been picked up by Sergeant Pearson. De- tective Freeborough felt sure the axe head was some- where close to the spot, and he volunteered to assist in the search, with the result above mentioned. The axe head was found driven into the soil some five or six inches. It was en the hedge cop, about a dozen yards from the place where the trap was stopped, just inside the field on the right hand side of the road. The axi head has the broken portion of the shaft remaining in the socket, and was covered with blood stains, and a quantity of hair was adhering to it. PRISONERS BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

At the Crewe Police Court, on Thursday, Richard Davies and George Davies were again charged with the mui der of their father, near the village of Hough on the 25th January. The court was again crowded. Mr. Stuart Brooke prosecuted. Sarah Ann Leach, widow, Victoria-st., Crewe, deposed that at eight o'clock on the evening of the 25th ult., George Davies purchased at her shop a box of gun caps. Richard went later and bought gunpowder. Inspector Oldham proved finding the axe head. It was proved that the axe had been taken from the de- ceased's shop at Victoria-st., Crewe. Mary Davies, mother of the prisoners, deposed to the custom of her late husband driving from his place of business at Hough with Georgie, whilst Richard usually walked home. Both Richard and George appeared to be on good terms with their father; and as to the other members of the family, witness said, "We made our- selves comfortable." Dr. Matthews, Nantwich, deposed that the wounds on the deceased's head might have been caused by the hatchet. Detective-inspector Brittain deposed to finding gun- powder in the stable, and in the kitchen of the de- ceased's shop in Crewe two pistols, one loaded, and a re- volver with six chambers loaded. He found gun caps and cartridges in an overcoat. Prisoners were committed to Chester Ast•izes for trial.

WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL.
GIFT OF A SCHOLARSHIP.

We have pleasure in stating that Mrs. Beamont. of Orford Hall, has intimated to the Governors of the Warrington Grammer School that she is desirous. of founding a scholarship of £5O per annum to either of the Universities of Oxford or Cambridge in connection with the Grammar School. This munificent gift is offered in memory of her late husband Mr. William Beamont who had written a history of the school and who was for many years one of the Governing Body of the Foundation, and whose son—afterwards Fellow of Trinity College,„ Cambridge—was one of its brightest ornaments.

div.head: INFLUENZA EPIDEMIC.
div.p: THE INFLUENZA EPIDEMIC.

The influenza is making terrible ravages throughout- the Mexican Republic. In the city of Mexico on Sun- day the deaths from this malady numbered 143. The Dean of Llandaff, Dr. Vaughan, is suffering from a severe attack of Russian influenza.

Two deaths have occurred at Downpatrick from _ influenza, one of the victims being Inspector Dunne, of the Royal Irish Constabulary. Influenza is largely on the increase among the British troops stationed at Cairo, and it has commenced to attack the natives.

Lord Carnarvon, who has been suffering from a severe attack of influenza, was sufficiently recovered on Wed- nesday evening to dine with his family, but until the weather becomes milder he will not venture out of doors.

The Cuerden Mill, near Preston, of Messrs. G. and R. Dewhurst, at which 600 hands were employed, has been stopped owing to the heads of the departments and a number of the hands being prostrated with influenza. The epidemic is prevalent noir in the Preston district, and several people are crippled in consequence of the number of workpeople ill.
DISTRICT CONVENTION OF GOOD TESiFtARB:

The annual session of the District Convention of• Good Templars was held in the Congregational Schoolroom, Golborne, on Saturday afternoon. Bro. J. Lindon C.C.T., of St. Helens, presided and was supported by nearly all the Convention officers, as well as a large number of visitors from IN arrington, St. Helens, Earlestown, Ashton, Haydock and Gol- borne. Brother Morris Jones, D. Sec., of Liverpool, and Bro. R. D. Petterson, of Birkenhead, were received with Templar honours. The annual reports of.the officers were first read. Bro. E. Newman C.S., reported that the lodges and temples in the district were all full of life and the members were. doing what they could to bring outsiders into their ranks. Since their last annual meeting one temple and three lodges had affiliated themselves with the' Convention, which was now formed of ten lodges and seven temples. The reports from the lodges and temples showed an increased membership.—Bro. Geo. Clarke, C. Treas. dealt with the financial posi- tion of the Convention, and showed a balance in, hand after the payment of all liabilities.—Bro. Geo. Punshon reported on electoral matters as affecting the temperance question, and mentioned that at St. Helens temperance candidates had fought and won in the recent municipal elections. The reports were unanimously adopted and thanks were tendered to the officers for their services. The election of officers then took place and the following were appointed: C.C.T., Bro. Col. Sergeant Geo. Devlin, Warrington: C.Co.. Bro. John Vint, Ashton; C.S.J.T., Sister Elizabeth Clarke, Earlestown ; -C.E.S., Bro. Geo. Punshon. St. Helens; C.V.T.. SiAer A. Devlin„Warrington ; Bro. E. Newman, Earles- town; (T. Treas., Bro. Geo. Clarke, Earlestown; C. Chap.; Bro. J. Speakman, Ashton ; P.C.C.T., Bro. J. Lindon, St. Helens ; C.G., Bro. J. Blinstone, Ashton; C. Sent., Bro. J. Singleton, St. Helens; C.A. Sec., Bro. E. Jenkin.on. Earlestown; C.D. Mar., Sister S. Houghton, We.rringt on. . _ _

, A public tea meeting was afterwards held and a large number of friends attended. Bro. R. D. Petterson of Birkenhead presided, and he, with Bro. Morris Tones, D. Sec., of Liverpool, gave interesting addresses. The evening's programme of songs, recitations, readings, &c., was well rendered by Sisters L. Henshaw, U. Stirrup, Jane Clarke, Devlin, Elizabeth Clarke, A. Sheath: Brothers Geo. Clarke, Geo. Punshon, D. Whittle, E. Newman and J. Leather. Votes of thanks to the Chairman speakers and all who bad taken part, closed a successful entertainment.

ONE of the pleasantest and most Talks With Emerson. stimulating articles in the maga- zines for the current month appears in "The Century," under the title of "Emerson's Talks with a College Boy." The great American writer is now classed amongst the men Who have been; but he has woven such a spell Over his admirers that there is something almost enchanting in the bare suggestion of his talks With a college boy. Talk he did, though talking was not in his way, and the boy, now grown to • man, Mr. C. J. WOODBURY, has done a service to his kind in putting on record what he remembers • of his chats with the foremost thinker of his day. As might be expected, EMERSON wished to be useful to the college boy in his reading and in his studies,. and the talks are, therefore, in the nature of advice—advice of that gentle, high-toned spiritual kind which was characteristic alike of the poet and the man. As we have students amongst our readers who may not see "The Century," we ven- ture to extract a few pregnant sentences. EMER- SON says :—" The most interesting writing is that Which does not quite satisfy the reader: try to leave a little thinking for him. That will be better for both. The trouble with most writers is that they spread too thin. The reader is as quick as they; has got before, and is ready waiting." How ;true all this is must be obvious to every person of active mind who has found himself growing impa- ;tient of a prosy writer, and especially of a prosy , sPeaker, for the writer can be shut up, while the • speaker insists Upon being heard. EMERSON prac- tised what he preached; too faithfully, some say, for he occasionaly leaves to the reader more think- ing than he is capable of. Referring to the use of Words, he says :—" Pull them apart, see how they are made. Avoid the adjective. Let the noun do the work. The adjective introduces sound ; gives an unexpected turn, and so often mars with an 'unintentional false note." This is a good lesson ; but it is one hard to learn. The young writer "delights in the adjective ; for he likes sound, and tannot, until he has progressed in the art of ex- Pression, understand why he should avoid it. Then as to facts :—" You must know about owner- ‘BlllP hi facts; what another sees and tells you is not yours, but his. If you had seen it, you would not have seen what he did, and even less what lie As to reading :—" So learn to divine books, , `'° feel those you want without wasting much time 'Wer them; often a chapter is enough. The glance teveals when the gaze obscures. Somewhere the author has hidden his message. Find it, and skip the paragraphs that do not talk to you." Advice 15f this kind will doubtless startle conscientious . ,teaders who think that when they begin a book it : 4.3 their diity to read it through, line by line. But f thtY are wasting time when they wade through ' Pages that do not talk to them. It is said of Mr. Gladstone that he is a perfect master in the art of itl.)eading. He makes light even of heavy blue for he sees at a glance what is of use, and . What is not of use to him ; for there is, as Miler- : 11°ton remarks, " a great secret in knowing what ' I,..keeP out of the mind as well as to put in." 17ain :—" Information is nothing, but the man 1 . oehind, it. Yield not one inch to the forces which 7 ,"Ispire to make you an echo. That is the sin and . °grnatism of creeds. Avoid them; they liuild a 4e,teeabout the intellect." This, it may be said, is s.wele doctrine of free thought. So it is, and it [. iscquires to be preached more and more. He is the ia , t 17° of slaves who dare not think for himself. freedom of thought does not mean freedom Lre'rri duty. Let the reader weigh this: "By work- doing for others simultaneously with the doing ;rll37olar own work, you make the greatest gain. kat iS the generous giving or losing of your life Zl'leh saves it." This, as we understand it, is the *4, is of true religion, and of true politics; and rcl`'eu the doubt comes which we cannot dispel we 10.114 " wait," as EMERSON says, "until to-morrow 2tning." ;low serenely, how sincerely and how 'ls* he makes his criticism of life! It hasbroken out amongst the school children of Frodsham ; and there has been one death, from) the disease at Warrington, besides a considerablunumber of sufferers. It may bean very well for those who havan't had the malady to make light of it;. but the sneezers say it is "not to be sneezed at."

It would seem that the Government have got scar- ed on the question of Free Education.. The clericals, combining with old-fashioned Tories, have put on the screw ;and the chances are that the Budget surplus will go in another,. and perhaps a, worse way. With Free Education, as with Home Rule, it is now merely a matter of time, and the hour will he struck with the return to power of the Liberal party.

It is stated that there is now a fair opportunity of the Warrington Corporation becoming pos- sessed of the Waterworks. The Sub-Committee of the Town Council will recommend their acquisi- tion upon the basis of 30 years' purchase upon the maximum dividends. Thirty years' purchase is a big sum ; but, if it does not mean more than the Company would be likely to get under arbitration, it will be better to settle privately than to resort to a compulsory, and what may prove, a costly pro- cess.

We have long been strongly of opinion that the water for a town should be in the possession of the town. And now is the time to stir, when there is a prospect of Warrington making a step forward. Let the Corporation take the ratv'epayers into their confidence, and, if they are doing the right thing, they will be well supported. An esteemed corres- pondent under the title of "Junius" contributes an important article on the subject, which will be found in another column.

If the uses of adversity are sweet, the abuses of prosperity are bitter. The drink bill for 1888 was £124,000,000; trade is better, drinking has in- creased, and the consequence is that the total for 1889 is I:132,000,000. The revenue, of course, gains by such folly--a circumstance which caused Cowper to exclaim— Drink and be mad then ! 'Tis your country bids: Gloriously drunk, obey the important call;. Her cause demands the assistance of your throats; Ye all can swallow, and she asks no more.

How children love their dolls! And the affection is no new thing. Some time ago there was dis- covered, in old Rome, the skeleton of a girl, and besides her in the coffin there was found a r erfectly modelled oak doll. In view of a revelation of this kind, it is scarcely possible to agree with Arch- bishop Trench, great as is his authority, in baying that the word doll was not introduced into the English language until after the time of Dryden. If there were dolls it, Rome 2,000 years ago, we may reasonable infer that there have been dolls in England for over a thousand years.

It was Calvin, was it not ? who preached the horrible doctrine that there are unbaptized "chil- dren in hell a span long." Strange as it may seem, the father of the liberal-minded Henry Ward Beecher held a like belief. Somebody has hunted up a passage to the following effect "That child who might have been an angel in heaven is now, through the negligence of its parents in the matter of baptism, a tenant in hell." It is some- thing gained that we do not hear of present-day ministers blaspheming in this precious style.

Shakespere bye-the-bye turns the tables in "Hamlet," upon the priest who says it would "profane the service of the dead to say a requiem" over the remains of "the fair" Ophelia, who has committed suicide. He makes her brother " Laertes " say in language as beautiful as it is forcible:—

Lay her i' the earth ; And from her fair and unpolluted flesh Let violets spring ! I tell thee, churlish priest, A ministering angel shall my sister be, When thou hest howling. Shakespere cannot be supposed to agree with all the utterances of his creations; but we know him sufficiently well to be assurei that he had no sympathy with intolerance.

-- The War Office have refused the application for a loan of £12,000 for a combined Rifle Range for the Manchester, Warrington, and other Lanca- shire Volunteers; but it is understood that the authorities are considering what other course can be taken. The country ought to be glad to give volunteers all the help they need. The way in which they are sent from pillar to post for the needful is discreditable to a rich nation which is spending over £30,000,000 on the army and navy. The abolition of a number of absurd pensions would provide ample funds for the requirements of our volunteers.

The landlord of the Hop'Pole Inn, Warrington, seems to have been "caught on the hop" whilst permitting gambling in his house during the small hours of the morning. He was fined 20s. and costs, but, by way of encouraging him to try again, his license was not endorsed. The Bench were even more considerate in dealing with those who wereH charged with aiding and abetting, for the case 1 against them was dismissed. It is just a little puzzling to those who haven't a knowledge of these things, to understand how the landlord could be guilty if the so-called aiders and abettors were innocent. Will somebody explain?

With regard to the suggestion of Mr. John Morley that a peer might be allowed to abandon his seat in the House of Lords and become eligible as a candidate for a seat in the Commons, Lord Derby points out that, if such a course were per- mitted, it would have a tendency to weaken the Upper House. But this difficulty might, he thinks, be met by the creation of life peers. The quantity could of course be maintained in this way, but what of the quality ? The Lords who made their way into the Commons would be able men; but could the same be said of life peers ? It would, we are inclined to think, be a case of surrendering eggs, and obtaining egg shells. But what then ? The weaker the House of Lords the better for the nation.

THE LEGE BILLIARD CHALLENGE' Cop. The competition for the billiard challenge cup, presented by Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P., for competition among the Conservative clubs of the Newton Division was advanced a stage last Saturday, when Penketh played their match with Rainbill, at ltainhill. The game resulted in favour of the home team, Penketh thus being thrown out of this year's contest. Winwick, whet) were drawn against St. Helens, have, it is stated had a walk over, owing to the the fact that ht. Helens were unable to send a team to meet them at WarringtOn on Saturday Hunaximes RE-COVERED at an hours' notice.—J. & W. lint ton, Sankey-street. MINERS' WAGES. In accordance with the resolution of the Bir- mingham Conference that an advance of ten per cent, be asked for by all miners throughout the kingdom, deputations of St. Helens miners waited upon the masters in the district a few days since to receive their reply to the circulars which had been sent to them asking for the advance. The replies generally were to the effect that, should themasters throughout South West Lancashire agree to con- cede another ten Der cent, they will do the same. 1 The miners intend to send in formal notices to ter- minate all contracts in a fortnight if their demand is not complied with. THE ASIITON-IN-MARERFIELD RECTOR AND HIS

DOG. At the Wigan Police Court, on Friday, the Rev.. W. J. Melville, rector of Ashton, was summoned for allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled.—The Rector appeared and admitted the offence. He said the dog had been driven mad through being re- peatedly muzzled and fastened up: it had since been destroyed. If he might be allowed to express his opinion on the muzzling of dogs he should have no—Mr. Eckersley : The charge against you is for having your (log at large.—The Rector: It is well known what the absurdities of the law are. lam not justifying my own action in any way. I could not help the dog escaping.—Mr. Eckersley: You will have to pay the costs. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at an hours' notiee.--Y. ,k W. Dutton, Sankey-street. "A Living Legacy" i an exciting story with a skilfully constructed plot. It vividly portrays the evils of fast life and betting; and will be found as wholesome as it is interesting.

div.head: B-LOCE ON THE LINE AT DITTON._
div.p: B-LOCE ON THE LINE AT DITTON._

The railway line between Ditton and Widnes on the London and North-Western Railway was blocked a couple of hours on Monday afternoon through a num- ber of waggons of a goods train leaving the metals from an unexplained cause. Passenger trains for Runcorn, Widnes and Liverpool were considerably delayed in con- sequence.

- Moss BANK WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES. The anniversary of this chapel was celebrated on Sun- day, when special services were held. The Rev. George Scott occupied the pulpit morning and evening. There were good congregations at each service, and collections were made in aid of the Trust Fund. On Monday evening a meeting was held under the auspices of the Band of Hope. An interesting programme of songs, re- citations, &c., was gone through by the members. Mr. S. B. Stringer presided.
- - BASINETTES, new designe.—Garland, Ironmonger, War- rington.—Advt.
SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.

Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, on Monday held an inquest at the Widnes Accident Hospital, on the body of John Conrov, aged 50 years, of 1, Eleanor-st., Widnes, who died on Wednesday from injuries received at Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co.'s Works on the pre- vious day.—John Kelly, of VI, Midwood-st., said on Tuesday, the 4th inst., the deceased was on the high level pushing a waggon to the hoist. From some cause or other the waggon fell down the hoist and the deceased followed alighting on the top of the waggon. He had deceased placed on a door and conveyed out of the works. There was a gate which was always closed when the cage of the hoist was down. The cage at the time of the accident was down. He had worked at Messrs. Gaskells for 13 years and he had never known the gate to be out of order, and be open when the cago was down.—Wm. Gilmore, of 22, Milton-St., gave corroborative evidence, and said the gate worked all right after the accident.— Miss Downe, matron of the Hospital, said the deceased was brought to that Institution, on Tuesday evening, and died next day. He was suffering from a fracture of the left shoulder and scalp wound and internal injuries. Dr. McDonnell attended to him. Deceased never gave witness an account of how the accident occurred.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death, owing to the working of the hoist being defective." - PRIMITIVE METHODIST COAVENTION AT RUNCORN. On Saturday, a convention of ministers, officials, and members of -the Preston Brook Primitive Methodist Circuit, and neighbouring circuits. took place in Green- way-road Chapel, Runcorn. In the afternoon a "Session " was held, under the presidency of the Rev. C. Finch, of Runcorn. The Rev. W. Graham, of War- rington, read a paper prepared by Mr. D. Lewis, of Widnes (who was unable to be present), on "Evangel- istic work, past and present." A discussion in which the Revs. W. Evans (Lymm), W. Graham, and others took part ensued, and a resolution was unanimously passed, thanking Kr. Lewis for his paper and requesting I him to take steps to have it published. Subsequently I tea was provided in the vestry, and in the evening a I meeting was held in the chapel. Mr. F. J. Norman presided, and the Rev. R. Robinson, g Earlestown, read an excellent paper on " Reading in relation to the for- mation of character." An address on "Recreation" was also delivered by the Rev. W. Graham, who referred in particular to the influence football and other sports were having on the Churches and Sunday schools. A hearty vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman and to the, speakers. in consequence of important and pressing connexional work, the Rev. W. Graham ex- pressed a wish to be released from the duties of secretary, land the Rev. W. Evans wag elected to /In the position. It was decided to hold the next session at Lymm. •

DANGEROUS PRACTICES ON THE RAILWAY AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Mr. H. Wade Deacon, Mr. J. Birchall, and Mr, T. S. Timmis, a boy named Oswald Cunliffe, whose home is in Walmsley- st., was summoned for having, on the 19th January, unlawfully and maliciausly removed the breakpins of three waggons situate in the Widnes dock siding of the London and North-Western Railway Company, with intent to upset, overthrow, or injure the waggons.—Mr. Preston, solicitor, prosecuted and stated that on the Sun- day previous to the committal of this offence, an empty van standing in the siding was set on fire. 32 empty casks wiire rolled into the canal, from the wharf, a large liron bolt was drawn from the dock stage, and the gage glasses of four or five cranes were smashed. In conse- quence, on the day in question detectives were set to watch the place, and about noon the defendant trespassed on the line near the Iron Bridge, and removed the break- pins.from three waggons in a manner that shaweci it was not the first time he had done such work. The object of the Company was not so much to punish this boy as to bring before the public the danger there was in such conduct, and draw attention to the fact that the offence was punishable with penal servitude.—The mother of the boy promised that he should I3e soundly whipped, and the Bench having seriously remonstrated with the boy, Mr. Preston withdrew the charge.—Wil- Ham Manning (15), Charles Manning (13), Ernest Thomas Ankers (11), and Robert Yates (13), were charged with trespassing on the line on the same date, and a similar course was followed with these defendants, with the exception of Ankers, who was unreservedly dismissed. Warrington WIDNES TRADERS' ASSOCIATION. . . .

The annual meeting of the members of this Asso- ciation was held in the Lunch-room, at Messrs. Gaskell and Deacon's works, on Friday last. Mr. E. K. Muspratt, J.P., presided, and there were present Messrs. T. Sutton Timmis, J.P., H. Gaskell, Jun., J.P., J. Brock, J.P., and H. Wade Deacon, J.P. (hon. sec.)—The Secretary submitted the 'anaual report, which stated that in conjunction with the Local Board, the Committee objected to certain alterations which the Manchester Ship Canal Company proposed to make in their plans, and maintained that under their Act of Parliament the company was obliged to cut away more of the rock on the Widnes side of the river, near Runcorn Bridge, than they showed their intention of do- ing on the plans deposited under the Act with the Mer- sey Conservancy. Interviews were held with Mr. Leader Williams on behalf of the Canal Company, and an inter- view was also held with Admiral Richards, the acting conservator of the Mersey. The Canal Company had ' that year lodged a Bill, the object of which was to authorise the making of certain modifications in the original plans. The Committee, with the Committee of ! the Local Board, had met and considered the proposals,l and recommended that a petition be lodged against the Bill, unless satisfactory arrangeinents were previously made with the Canal Company. In accordance with the Provisions of the Railway and Canal Traffic Act, 1888, the railway companies duly lodged their proposed clas- sification and schedule with the Board of Trade. The classification proposed was a uniform one for all the rail- ways. hut each company proposed its own set of rates. The Committee considered the matter very fully, and decided that on the general question it would not lodge an objection, but would work with and subscribe to the funds of the Railway and Canal Traders,' Association. That policy had been carried out, and the President and Honorary Secretary had attended several conferences to! represent the views of the association. The main point of interest to the Widnes traders was the proposed re- I peal by the London and North-Western Railway Corn- ! nano of the special sections intmiluced for the protection of the traders of the St. Helens Railway in the Acts of 1884, 1885, and 1E67. Those clauses were ins.rted in the I !Acts onlyafter the greatest efforts on the part of the traders, and it was clearly impossible to agree to the pronosed repeal. The etaueee were almost equally 110 partant to the St. Helens trident, and to some importers who used Garston Dock. The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report, said as regarded the Manchester Ship Canal Company. the report itself expiained the action ef the Committee. With respect. to the Railway and Canal Traffic Act of 1838, he noticed that before the Board of Trade inquiry a statement had been made -,n behalf of the railway companies that traders had given no a.sisfanne whatever in classification of Mr. Thnmis.—Who made that allegation ?—The Chair- man.—One of the counsel. Ilethought it was abeolare- ly untrue as it regarded the Widnes traders. He moved that the report of the Executive Com- mittee ;be received and adapted, and that printed copies be circulated amongst the members.— Mr. Timmis seconded the resolution, w!.;ich was adopted: ' —Mr eon mquestion upon the of the Ship Canal - , • Dea ' Company the association had had their attention drawn to the piling going on in the river on the Runcorn side, and to the company not getting out the rock sufficiently on the Widnes side. They objected to other alterations proposed to be made, and the Committee, in conjunction with the Local Board, were considering the matter,and if not settled a iiicably between them they would take action and oppose them. It was resolved thit the action of the Executive Committee, with regard to the proposals of the Manchester Ship Cereal Company, be approved, and that a petition be lodged against the Bill unless satis- factory arrangemsnts are previously made with the com- pany. The Meeting also authorized the Committee to subscribe a third of any costs incurred by the Widnes Local Board in opposing the Ship Canal Bill, provided that such portion shall not exceed £lOO. It was further resolved, that the action of the Committee in connection with the proposed classification and t-chedule of maxi- mum rates and charges lodged by the railway companies with the Board of Trade be approved. The financial statement shows the association to be in a flourishing condition, the balance in hand being £272 3s. 11d. After meeting all the charges against the association there will be a balance of £153 17s. 4d.—Mr. E. K. Muspratt (president) and Mr. H. Wade Deacon (hon. secretary) were unanimously re-elected for the next three years, and a vote of thanks having been accorded to them for their past services, the meeting terminated.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the members of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at the Work- house at Dutton. on Tuesday, when there were pre- sent—Colonel Ashton (in the chair) the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. 11. J. Grine, S. Taylor, T. Lewis, J. Stokes. J. Baguley. J. Jeffs, Turner, Brandreth, D. Jones, Bretherton, Wilkinson, Heywood, W. Whitlow, Forster, 11. Linaker (clerk), and B. G. Linaker (deputy clerk). ITIE SCHOOLMASTER. • A letter was read from the Local Government Board with repent to the appointment of Mr. R. Naylor to the post of schoolmaster at the Workhouse, and asking that the Board should make the term of notice three months instead of one for the first vear.—Mr. Stokes gave notice that he shoula move that Mr. Naylor be appointed on those terms. It seemed, however, ridiculous, and a pity that the appointment could not be amended with- out all that nonsense.—Mr. Whitldw Honour and obey, Mr. Stokes. (Laughter). THE COUNTY COUNCIL'S DEMAND. A communication was read from the Clerk to the Cheshire County Council acknowledging the receipt of a letter from the Guardians enclosing a copy of a resolu- tion to the effect that the Council be asked to permit the call for £4,870 which was required to be paid by the Ist of March to be deferred until the end of April. The writer stated that he had no authority to consent to the payment being deferred beyond the date of the precept, which must be complied with—Mt. Brandreth said that he would suggest that before the Board should meet the call he should It the County Council take pro- ceedings.—Mr. Taylor was of the same opinion, as the County Council had not acted very courteously towards that Board. Be felt very strongly on the matter, and maintained that it was one of the inost unreasonable demands that had ever been made.— Mr. Brandreth subsequently altered his resolution to the effect that the precept being prepared to meet the demands of the County Council be not signed, and that the Board calculate, and see how much they could pay on account of the £4,870 by the first of March, and send it to the County Council.—Mr. Jeffs seconded the proposition, which was unanimously carried.

VOTE OF THANKS. A cordial vote of thanks was passed to Mr. S. Taylor for his kindnes in giving a number of " Graphics " and other pagers for the use of the inmates. This was the whole of the business of importance.

RUNCORN SOAP AND ALKALI CONfPANY. The 24th annual ordinary general meeting of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company, Limited, was held on Monday, in the Law As-lodation Rooms, Cook-st. Mr. A. P. Pletcher (chairman) presided, and there was a good attendance.—Tne report, from which the following are extracts, was taken as read :—" The gross profits, including transfer fees. amount to £6,355 15s. 6d., from which must be de- ducted office expenses, salaries, commissions, rate., in- come tax, audit, &c., £3,907 17s. 10(1., and bank com- missions and balance of trade di.counts, &c., £1,4841 Os. 11d., leaving a balance of £963 16s. 9d. ; add to that amount the balance from last year (after payment of directors' fees) of £5,864 16s. 7d., which leaves an avail- able balance of £6,838 13s. 4d., which it is proposed to carry forward to next year. 'rhe past year has been a disappointing one for the alkali trade, and, with the ex- ception of bleaching powder, nearly every article of manufacture has failed to .realise ecst. In view of the possible break up of the Bleaching Powder Association, it was deemed prudent to improve, renovate, and make such additions to the plant and premises generally, as would conduce to the fullest workin, of the business under the most favourable conditions, and at the lowest possible cost. For these purposes an outlay of over £15,000 was incurred, and to that extent affected the re- sults of the year. The : Right Rev. Dr. O'Reilly, Bishop of Liverpool, presided, and delivered a speech, in which he impressed upon the audience the necessity of making provision for the poor ' Catholic children in workhouses and workhouse schools. —Dean Finegan moved" rhat this meet rig is of opinion that the establishment of a Poor Law School for the purpose of receiving children from the workhouse and bringing them up under Catholic guidance is a work of vital importance, and claims the support of the Catholics of this diocese."—The motion was seconded by Father Chapman, and carried.—A subscription list was opened and £7l 12s. was promised, £37 10. i. being handed in in cash.

div.head: INQUEST AT WIDNES.
div.p: INQUEST AT WIDNES.

Yesterday Mr W. T. Husband,deputy Coroner, held an inquest, at Widnes Police Court, on the bcdy of Sarah Elizabeth Susanah Rowhotham, 50 years of age, a mar- ried woman, of Pool-st., who died on Monday morning' from congestion of the liver and dropsy. It appeared that the woman had suffered from dropsy, in the left legand foot, for about 18 months, and on the night of the Eth June last year she, on her way to visit a rela- tive in Alfred-st., fell in a ditch. When taken out it was found that both her ankles were broken, and that her left foot was fractured. After some months she was again able to walk about the house, but three weeks ago she again became very unwell and died at noon on Tuesday. Dr. O'Neil certified that death was acceler- ated by the injuries.—A verdict of" Died from conges- tion of the liver and dropsy" was returned. Charles W. Ray, of Crow Wood, was summoned beforel the Widnes magistrates. to show cause why he should not contribute towards the support of his wife, Elizabeth Ray, who is chargeable to the common fund of the Pres- ent Union. Mr. J. Treary, the relieving officer, stated that the defendant's wife was removed to Rainhill Asy- lum on the 21st of June last. She cost the ratepayers Bs. 2d. per week, and as the defendant was earning an average of 28s. at Messrs. Sullivan's works, and had no young children to keep, the Guardians ordered him to pay 3s. Bd. per week. The defendant had, however, never paid more than 2s. 6d. per week, and he was, £1 us. 6d. in arrear.—The defendant said he could not keep a house over his head and pay more than 2s. 6d. He had recently been unfortunate in having his married daughter and her husband at home.—Mr. Deacon said 3s. 6d. was a very reasonable amount, and the magis- trates made an order accordingly. LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE RAILWAY COMPANY.

The half-yearly meeting of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company was held on Wednes- day. Mr. G. J. Armyte.ge, chairman of the Board, said the half year had been o.ne of prosperity. There had been an increase of £82,645 in the re- ceipts, balanced by an increase of expenditure of .£54,000. The higher prices of fuel and advanced wages were the main causes of the larger expendi- ture. Mr. Armytage thought that the dividend de- clared (4f per cent.) was satisfactory, considering the fact that the improvement in trade had not affected the cotton industry to anything like the same extent as the coal and iron industries. The report was adopted vt ithout serious criticism. .Sln. T. E. alas, M.P._

div.head: FINANCIAL POSITION OF RUNCORN UNION.
div.p: THE FINANCIAL POSITION OF RUNCORN UNION.

The financial statement for the Runcorn Union for the half-year ended Michaelmas last (certified by Mr. John Dolby, the Government auditor), has just been issued. We extract the following figures. The balance in favour of the Union at the commence- ment of the half-year was £4,483 12s. Bd., and the contributions made amounted t, £7,089 ; other receipts reached £545 14s. 11d., making the total receipts £12,120 15s. Od. The expenditure included common charges, £6,121 12s. id. (an increase of £1,976 95.), separate charges £36105. 9d. ; workhouse loan and interest repaid £lO9 13s. 4d. ; county rate, £2,193 6s. 2d. (in- crease £230 195.) ; a total expenditure of £8,461 2s. 4d., and there WAR a balance in hand of £3,659 12s. Bd. The outstanding liabilities of the Board amounted to £2,923 63. 2d., of which a proportion was on salaries account. The rateable value of the Unionl is £217,098 a decrease of £6,438 as compared with the corresponding half of last year. From particulars of common charges, we glean that in-maintenance cost £6ll 8s 3d., and out-relief £1,992 14s. 6d., and non-resident relief £2O 9s. 3d. Lunatics were &burden to the extent of £382 7s. 7d. Salaries or other remuneration of officers amounted to £529 lOs id. Vaccination was responsible for an item of £62 13s. 4d. and registration £73 18s Od. Amongst other charges the Assessment Committee is responsible for no less an expen- diture than £2503 5s 5d ,the great proportion of which,cer- tainly £2OOO, can be set down to the expense attending the Ship Canal appeal. In regard to the same matter it is pleasing to notice that Runcorn Overseers have been repaid £530 19s sd, which they had handed over on a call made on the increased assesment of the Ship Canal property, which was reduced in consequence of the appeal.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday. .Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., presided, and there were present Messrs. E. Carey, T. Handley' D. Wright, J. Nlidwood, H. Timmis, F. Liddell, F. Ileyes, J. Taylor, 11. Gaskell junr., J. Houghton, T. Sadler, J. T. Allen (clerk).

RESIGNATION OF THE SURVEYOR. The Surveyor (Mr. T. Higginson), handed in his resig- nation, which stated that he shou d terminate his duty on the 13th April.—The resignation was unanimously acceptee, and it was arranged to hold a special meeting on the 3rd March to appoi,,t a successor.

THE COMING ELECTION. The Clerk said it was necessary to appoint returning officer and assistants for the coming election. The Chairman was returning officer in virtue of his office, but if he became a candidate he could not act.—Mr. Gaskell moved that Mr. Mid wood be requested to act as returning officer. He had the experience and all the qualifications necessary and was a gentleman they could all trust to see that the election was carried on in a manner as satisfactory as possible.—Mr. Houghton seconded the motion.—The Chairman said perhaps it would be best to state at once that he intended to be a candiaate at the election.—The motion was carried unanimously.—Mr. Midwood acknowledged the appoint- ment and said he would try to do his duty.—Messrs. Lewin, Goff, Allen, Hoyle, Wilson, Heyes, Whitfield, Sankey, Hughes, Hackney, and 15 constables were appointed to assist the returning officer. PAIILIANENTAItY OPPOSITION. It was resolved that the chairman attach the seal of the Board to petitions against the Ship Canal Bill and the Brine Scheme Bill.
A LOAN.
A letter was road from t7f);--Local Government Board sanctioninz the borrowing by the Board of the sum of £4OO for the purpose of stables. . -

div.head: INFECTIOUS DISEASE.
div.p: INFECTIOUS DISEASE.

The Local Government Board wrote approving the order of the Local Board extending the application of the Infectious Diseases (Notification) Act, 1889, to measles and whooping cough. WAttNiNG TO PROXENLDRES. The Clerk reported that considerable darnago to property had been done on West Bank promenade. Seats had been broken and in many instances there was nothing but the iron framework left. Ile had written to Mr. Johnson, superintendent of police, who said the matter should receive attention.—lt was resolved to repair the seats, and to place a notice board in a conspicuous place stating that anybody damaging the Board's property would be liable to prosecution.

div.head: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE,
div.p: GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE,

The minutes of Committee stated that the mean rainfall for the month was 2.805 inches. The water in stock was 6,537.132 gallons. The illumin- ating power of the gas had averaged 1941. candles during the month. The wages required during the next four weeks for the Gas and Water Works was £lO5 per week. The Committee recommended that placards be issued offering a reward of 20s. for such information as would lead to the conviction of any persons damaging straet lamps. Mr. D. H. Lowryclaimed the sum of £5 ss. forinjuries received through falling into an open trench in Lugsdale-rnad, and the Committee recommended that the sum of £33s. Od. be offered to him in settlement of his claim without prejudice.—Mr. R. Collinwood (agent of Mrs. Stapleton Bretherton), was granted the privilege of shooting over Pex Hill for one year on payment of a sum of £s.—Mr. Wright moved the adoption of the minutes and drew attention to the large number of street lamps wilfully smashed, and wished the press to make puhlic the proceedings the Committee intended to take. —Mr. Gaskell seconded the motion, and stated that during the last three months, although they had made less gas than previously, the consumption of gas had been greater by about a million cubic feet. This was due to the fact that they had less loss from leakage than they had before. Not holy did it show that the mains and pipes were in very good condition, but that there WM no loss by condensation from the Dinsmore process. The actual loss of gas was only four per cent.—The minutes were passed. HIGHWAY MATTERS,-COUNTY COUNCIL INACTION._

The Highway Committee had received a letter from Mr. W . T. Husband, hon. secretary to the Widnes Con- servative, stating that the triangular piece of land in front of the Club would only be given up to the public upon the Board flagging the same. The Com- mittee recommended that the offer be accepted, the land to be dedicated to the public use—and the tender of W. F. Chadwick, on schedule of prices. about £44, be accep- ted for flagging. paving, &c., in front of the club and Drill Hall. Messrs. T. Holton and Sens, wrote asking if the Bard would object to the closing of Peel-st. if they purcha.Sed the adjoining property. The Committee In- structed the Clerk to reply tint the Committee would favourably entertain the scheme. The clerk to the County Council had written stating the Council declined to interfere with regard to the Gorsey-lane encroach- ments. With regard to the Moss Bank sewer several letters had been received from Messrs. S. Cowburn and Sons, and it was recommended that an engineer be ap- pointed to check the contractor's account,with full power to open out the work when required.----Mr. Sadler moved, and Mr. Houghton seconded, the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Gaskell said the County Council, being a House of Landlords, there was always a suspicion that they would act favourably towards landowners, and he should like to know the reason why the Council declined to interfere in Gorsey-lane.—Mr. Wright opposed the recommendation of the Committee with regard to Moss Bank sewers, and said there was a strong' public opinion on the question.—Mr. Sadler replied that no reason was assigned by the County Council why they declined to interfere in Gorsey-lane. He saw no reason why the letter should not be read. As to Mr. Wright's statement, the strong feel- ing was very limited. The Committee could not pass this account as it stood, and they had no other course open to them than to call in an engineer to check it.— The letter from the Clerk to the County Council was read as follows :—" I brooght your letter of the 28th ult, before the Main Roads and Bridges Committee at their last meeting, when Mr. Snape explained the nature of the alleged encroachment upon the waste land adjoin- ing the highway separating the townships of Widnes and Cuerdley, and after some discussion the Committee passed a resolution declining to entertain the matter.—Mr. Gaskell : They give us no reason for their refusal to pro- tect publi.: rights. They simply give us a bare refusal, nothing else, and I think this letter ought to go forth to ' the public.—The minutes were adopted. HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The Medical *Officer reported to the Health Com- mittee that during the past month there were 101 births, and 63 deaths, being at the respective rates of 40.4 and 25.2 per 1,000. The death-rate although so high, includes only one death or

O 4 per 1,000 from zymotic disease, 23 deaths were due to pneumonia aud bronchitis, many of them who fell victim to these maladies being in the prime of life. Thirty-three cases of infectious diseases have been re- ported, in one instance when there was no medical man in attendance. I found, on inspection, that a patient was not suffering from measles, as was supposed, nor from any infectious disease.—Mr. Wright reported having received the following donations for the fever hospital;. W. Farrant, £4 ;T. Ireland, 10s. ; T. Robinson, 10s. ; k rkes, 10s.'• W. Wood, 10s. ; T. Minton, 10s. ;J. I- -man, ; total £7, which had been expended upon Chat ‘rticles at the Hospital. The London and North useful 'lilway Co.'s employees had also given a dona- Western n. to the Charity Fund. The donors were tion of £2 7s.
