div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANg.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANg.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at the Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday afternoon, when there were present the Bev. Dean Fine- gan (chairman), Messrs. W. Tyrer, W. Middlehurst,j. W Wareing, G. Davies, J. Burchall, J. Ellison G. E. Chadwick, J. Marsh, J. Kenwright, J. Leatherbarrow, C. B. Johnson, W. Lowe, E. Syder, J. Griffiths, H. ' Hulme, E. Birchall, J. Peover, W. Daine, J. Whalley, It. A. Graves J. Mercer, P. Loßgton, J. Groldsworth, and S. H. Hartley (elerk). lanuars.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 589 inmates of the house this week, 600 last week, and 608 in the corresponding week last year. 'MR ST. HELENS RELIEF OFFICES.—The Building Com- mittee had considered the draft plans of proposed new relief offices at St. Helens, and inspected the land pro- posed to be acquired from the Society of Friends for that parpose. The Committee resolved that the scheme be not proceeded with any further, and it was decided that steps should be taken for the alteration and adaptation of the present offices.—The minutes of the Committee were approved, on the motion of Mr. Middlehurst, se- conded by Mr. Burchall COLLECTORS' STATEMENTS.—The Clerk submitted the statements from the collectors' during the past month, and stated that those of Mr. Parkinson for Eccleston showed that there was a sum of £2,327 13s. still to be collected for Eccleston and £261 16s. sa. for Knowsley before the end of the financial year. From that amount were to be deductions for empty property and com- pounding of rates.—ln reply to Mr. Marsh, the Clerk stated that the financial year ended on the 25th March next.

ESCAPH OF LUNATICS FROM RAINHILL ASYLUM/L-I'6e Clerk reported that a deputation from the Board had visited Rainhill County Asylum and saw the whole of the patients chargeable to the Union, whom they found I clean in their persons and well-dressed. In the visitors' book at the institution the Guardians made the following entry: The attention of the Guardians has been directed 1 to the escape of patients from the asylum and, without reflecting upon the mangement of the institution they think that such care should he constantly exercised, and, if necessary, other means adopted as would preclude the possibility of the life and comfort of any member of the community being endangered by the irresponsible acts of those unfortunate persons who are committed to the charge of the asylum authorities." In reference to that matter he (the Clerk) had received a letter from Dr. Wigglesworth, the medical superintendent of the Asylum, in which he wrote "There have been a few escapes from the Asylum lately (as, indeed, has always been ths case), the escapes having chiefly been affected from working parties, and in all cases, by harmless patients. As, however, no persons life has been placed in even the smallest danger by an escaped patient, as, indeed, nobody has been assaulted in any kind of way by anyone of them, lam somewhat at a loss to understand what the Guardians referred to by their observations under this head." Continuing, the Clerk said the remarks of the Guardians as expressed in the visitor's book were intended to be brought under the notice of the Visiting Committees of the Asylum. It had come to the knowledge of the Guardians that some important ratepayers of the Union had been subject to great inconvenience and annoyance by frequent escapes from that public institution and they felt themselves bound to take the first opportunity of drawlng attention to it. They thought something should be done to prevent a recurrence.—The Chairman said he approved the action of the deputation and while not reflecting in the least up,n the management of the Asylum, he thought the Guardians were doing perfectly right in seeking to protect those who lived in the vicinity of the institution. He moved a resolution that the Board approve of the remarks and action of the deputation.— Mr. J. Wareing seconded.—After some further discussion the resolution was unanimously carried. . . . .
This was the whole of the btisiness.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. "Br AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT."

The Surveyor of Whines Local Board, Mr.T.lliggin- son, has acquiesced in the inevitable and handed in his resignation. but a number of his friends have held an " indigation meeting" and have appointed a committee to draw up a petition calling upon the Chairman of the Board to convene a public meeting of ratepayers to protest against the injustice suffered by the surveyor. A 8 the Board was almost unanimous in requesting Mr. Higginson to resign, and arrange- ments have been made for appointing his successor at a salary of .£250, or £5O less than that now paid, it is not likely that the prayer of the petition will be acceded to. In the course of a few weeks the annual election of five members of the Board takes place, and the retiring member are warned that the contest will be made "rather hot" for them. It is to be hoped that the natural law of the "survival of the fittest" will hold good in this case The breach between Runcorn Guardians and Che- shire County Council appears to be growing wider with respect to the call for .£4670. The Guardians applied for an extension of the time allowed for finding the money; but from a communication read at the meeting on Tuesday, the officials of the C.C. would appear to have treated the application with scant Courtesy, and as unworthy o. being placed before the Council. The clerk merely states that he has no authority to extend the time. The Guardians were naturally annoyed at this rather scurvy treat- ment, and have retaliated by passing a resolution not to issue a precept for the money, but merely undertake a payment of about £2OOO on account. As the Council are indebted to Runcorn Union to the extent of a like sum, it is calculated that the difference then between them will only be slight, but it is to be feared that the Council will object to this rough and ready reckoning, and that the Guar- dians have embarked in a centest in which they will be worsted.

The explanation given by Mr. Speakman as to the cause of the very heavy call should be b-)rne in mind, and the blame placed in the proper quarter. Shortly, the County Council took over the adminis- tration of the County burdened with a heavy debt, which the magistrates, before vacating their posi- tion as administrators, should have wiped off by levying a special rate. Then the contribution from the Weaver Trust Fund was £5,000 less than in the previous year. Thus the new authority had not a clear start, and the money now demanded is a , necessary consequence.and as the Guardians will be compelled to find their proportion they may as well start about the work soon as late. The people who had the pleasure of attending to the course of lectures, at Runcorn, on" English Social Reformers," will be gratified at the elilogittms I passed upon them by the gifted lecturer, Mr. Hudson Shaw, in a report he has forwarded to the University. He was highly satisfied with the result of the lectures, and does not fail to give a meed of praise to the enthusiastic secretary, Mr. Wynne Humphreys, to whom the success of the organis- ation was so largely due.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

FREIL Cfruncii.—During the past week mission services have been held in the United Methodist Free Church, by Miss Abbott, of Manbfield, Notts. ASTON-Br-SurroN.—At a meeting of the Aston United District School Board, on Saturday, it was decided to enlarge the Aston Board School, at a cost of about £3OO, from the designs and under the superintendence of Mr. Samuel Davies, architect, of Frodsham. The executcrs of the late John Gleave are the contractors for the work, their tender having been accepted in a limited com- petition. ECCLICSIASTICAL Avvonivmavr.—The Rev. Frank D. Ring,rose, 8.A.. of Merton College, Oxford, has been recently appointed by the Vicar, Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., to the senior curacy of Frodshain, as a successor to the Rev. A. Grier. For the past three years Mr. Itingrose has been one of the curates of I.oleds Parish Church, where he worked at first with the present Bishop of Chester, and latterly with Dr. Talbot. He comes to the Frodsharn parish with high commedation from both the vicars under whom he has laboured.

div.head: REPORTED DEATH OF THE SULTAN OF ZANZIBAR.
div.p: REPORTED DEATH OF THE SULTAN OF ZANZIBAR.

ZANZIBAR, THURSDAY EVENING.—The Sultan's death took place at one o'clock. The cause is at present un- known, though it is learnt that his Majesty has been ail- ing during the last two days. In the course of the day the body was brought into the town from the Sultan's rural residence, and Dr. Charlesworth and Dr. Martin are to make an examination to-night, with the object of ascertaing the cause of death. The Sultan's brother Ali has already been elected to reign in his stead.
WIM

div.head: " THIS MAN WAS FRIGHTENED."
div.p: " THIS MAN WAS FRIGHTENED."

And on reading the facts it will appear that he had reason to be. The man referred to was Edward Perrin, a guard on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway. In September,lBB7, he met with an accident, which gave a temporary shock to his system. Not long afterwards he began to feel a pain in the chest and have difficulty in breathing, and threw up a great deal of mucus (phlegm.) He at once cencluded he had some serious ailment of the lungs, and sought medical advice. 'he doctor said it was so, and added that there was no cure for it, and he could do no more than give him something to ease the pain and the cough. Then the doctor gave Mr. Perrin a certificate stating that he was suffering from " Catarrh Phthisis," which is the professional term for that dread ul malady Consumption• Further symptoms soon appeared which seemed to con- fum this alarming opinion. Thepoor fellow experienced great pain in eating and a tightness across the chest, which felt, he said, "as if some strong man was grip- ping him around the body under the arms. The rest of Mr. Perrin's narrative is best related in his own words. He says:—" I soon commenced to have a brackish taste in the mouth as if I had been sucking copper. Then came cold chills and sweats in turn, the cough got hollow, and I raised more than I had done. These terrible symptoms so scared me that I went and consulted the late Dr. Dacre Fox, who was at that time Consulting Physician to the Railway Company and to the Infirmary. He examined me carefully, and certified as follows : "In the case of Guard Perrin. This man is evidently frightened. He is suffering from Pletkisis and Dyspepsia. Cod liver oil and iron are indicated." "This fully bore out what the other doctor had said, so I now looked upon myself as done for. I took every- thing I could hear tell of. I have drank gallons of cod liver oil a ad sherry, and have had many quarts of cam- phorated oil rubbed on my chest, until my wife was sick of rubbing. I was also poulticed continually, but in spite of all this terrific dosing and medicating I got gradually worse. In half-a-dozen words my con - dition was this: I believed myself to be fast going to the grave with consumption; my friends said so, the doctors said so ; and it looked like it if any- thing ever did. It is understood that consumption is :sure death, and I made up my mind for that awful end. I had been off my work from 1887 to 1888. I was ashamed to be away so much, as I was obliged to draw funds from the Club all the time to help to support my family. "While I was thus doing nothing but waiting to die, crawling about feebly like a man who is virtually done with this world, I happened one day to meet Inspector Rippon, of Ardwick Station, one of the Traffic Inspectors of our line. He was shocked at my looks, but said 'Perrin, I don't know as anything will help you, but if anything will, it is Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup.' I remember that this idea amused me, miserably broken and ill as I was. Help me! Could it cure consump- tion? Not likely. Impossible! Still it couldn't make me worse, and so I got a bottle and began to take it. I could scarcely credit my own feelings, but as sure as truth is truth, before I had used up that bottle of medi- cine, I found relief. Now comes what you may find it hard to believe—l took but two more bottles and went back to work, and have been sound and healthy ever since. I told the doctor about it, and although he saw I was well, he seemed displeased. You say Mother , Seigel's Syrup cured you ?' he said. "Nonsense. It is I only a quack medL:ine ; it is nothing but stuff and rub- bish.'Well, all right,' I said to myself, 'it may be stuff and rubbish, but it has made a sound man of me after that very doctor had me booked for the graveyard, and said no earthly power could keep me out of it.' That was enough for me, and will be enough for thousands of others in this country. "I am exposed to all sorts of weather, but have never had a return of the bad breathing, chest pains, nor any of the other symptoms that nearly frightened me out of my senses. I eat and enjoy my food as well as any man in England. Now what was the secret of this getting well ? If I really had consumption it was nothing short of a miracle, but I never had consumption at all. The doctors were all wrong in calling it that. What I actually suffered from was indigestion and dyspepsia, which causes the same symptoms that mark true consumption ; hence, lots of people who are sup- posed to have lung complaint might be as easily cured as I was if they would let cod liver oil alone and take Mother Seigel's Syrup." Mr. Perrin's address is—No. 27, Pollitt Street, off Hyde Road, Manchester, and he will reply to any letters Written to him concerning his case.

div.head: 13EFottg TAR MAGIsTRATEs.
div.p: 13EFottg TAR MAGIsTRATEs.

THE WINWICR-ST. OBSTRUCTION de-am. At the Warrington Police, Courty on Monday. Elizabeth Hallows, greengrocery and John Gregg,,, furniture broker, ' appeared to answer adjourned summonses charging ' them with having obstructed the footpath in Winwick- ' st. by exposing goods for sale thereon. It was stated that no further notice of the matter had been taken by either the Watch or the Markets Committee, and, as it appeared that the offence had not been repeated, the magistrates dismissed the cases. CHEATING THE CHESHIRE LINES COMMITTEE. On Wednesday, at the Warrington Police Court, a .voung fellow who gave the name of William Cecil Grimd- ley, and described himself as a sailor, was brought up in custody on a charge of having travelled on the Cheshire Lines Railway, from Hunts Cross to Warring- ton, on the day previous, without having paid the fare. He admitted that he had done so, and said that he was out of employment and was trying to make his way to Manchester. A fine of 10s. and costs, with the alter- native of a fortnight's imprisonment, was imposed. OVERCROWDING IN LODGING HOUSES. Two cases of overcrowding in lodging-houses were in quired into by the Warrington magistrates on Monday. Bridget Kimlin, of Dial-st., was fined 101. and costs for having kept more persons in her house than it was reg- istered for. Inspector Norman informed the Court that there were 25 people in the house, which was only registered for 18, and Inspector Powell said that two women were sleeping on chairs. William Stewart, of 12, Angel-yard, was also fined 10s. and costs, and it was stated that six persons, one being a girl of sixteen, had i been sleeping together n one corner of the room. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASE: A WARNING. William Spofford was summoned for having neglected to send his child to school. The case had several times been adjourned. M. Riley said that Mrs. Spofford, who persistently refused to bring the boy to court, had treated the authorities with the greatest contempt. Mr. A. Browne, who on a previousoccasion appeared for the defence, intimated that in consequence of what had since transpired he desired to wash his hands of the case. Mr. Riley asked the magistrates to deal with the defend- ant for the offence of refusing to produce the child in court, and they acceded, inflicting a penalty of 20s. including costs, or 14 days' imprisoment in default of payment.

div.head: MUZZLING ORDER.
div.p: THE MUZZLING ORDER.

At Warrington Police Court, on Monday, a labourer, I named William Smith, was summoned for having con- travened the recent Order of the Board of Agriculture with regard to the muzzling of dogs. Defendant pleaded that his dog was sufficiently muzzled, but evidence was given by a person named Walter Warburton to the effect that on the Ist inst., he was in Scotland-rd., when the dog bit him, although at the time it was wearing a muzzle. The animal was produced in Court, and Alder- man Harrison remarked that it was a benevolent looking one. The Magistrates' Clerk ruled that a dog that was not sufficiently muzzled was not in point of fact muzzled at all, and the Bench ordered the defendant to pay Bs. 6d. costs. lie said that he had bought a new muzzle. A LIVERPOOL LAD IN TROUBLE AT WARRINGTON.

'Nci-la-eil-S-ea. Is, (16), of Liverpool, whose parents are poor but respectable, ran away from home in November last; and has since then picked up a precarious living as a street singer. Last week he came to Warrington, and was arrested on a charge of felony, it being alleged that he had stotery a card of studs, of the value of 125., from a stall iathe Market kept •by Lewis Hart, a Liverpool Smallware deakr. He was brought before the magis- trates, and remanded to Saturday last, oa which day evidence was given by Constable Bell to the effect that he arrested' prisoner in the first instance on a charge of attempting to pick a lady's pocket, and that on being searched prisoner was found to have in his possession a card of studs, which had been reported as missing from Plart's stall. The magistrates sent him to prison for a month, with hard labour. TRE,RIORT WAY TO PUNISH BRUTALITY. William Farrel, a young man, who had been appre- hended under a Warrant, was brought before the War- rington magistrates, on Tuesday, on a charge of having assaulted his sister on the 27th of December last. Com- plainant gave evidence of the assault, and added that on different occasions prisoner had threatened her with a revolver and a razor. It also transpired that he had undergone a term of imprisonment for six months for having assaulted his aged mother, who now appeared in court and asked the Bench to let him off with a fine. Prisoner said that he had turned over a new leaf, and now had a chance of getting on in life, but the Bench

gave him the well merited punishment of imprisonment for three months, with hard labour. CURIOUS CHARGE OF TERM A young man named Joseph Jenks, who had been em- ployed in taking charge of a chipped potato machine, was charged at the Warrington Police Court, on Satur- day, with having, by means of a trick, stolen 11d., the money of a boy named George Unsworth, 13 years of age, who lives in nostock-st. It was alleged that the night before the defendant was in charge of the potato cart in Horsemarket-st. Unsworth asked bun for a half- pennyworth of potatoes. A few minutes afterwards Unsworth discovered that he had, by mistake, given Jenks a shilling instead of a halfpenny. This the latter denied, but some time afterwards Unsworth appeared with P.C. Clough, and defendant returned the money and asked Unsworth to say no more about it. The Bench said they were perfectly satisfied that Jenks had retained the money as long as possible, and fined him 55., or in default seven days' imprisonment. The money was paid.

VIOLENT ASSAULT ON AN UNOFFENDING POSTMAN. On Thursday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, a farm labourer named John Cunningham, forty years of age, was brought up in custody on a charge of having committed a violent assault upon William Brad- shaw, a postman. The affair took place on Wednesday night, in the neighbourhood of Friars-green. Bradshaw, whose face bore very eviderlt marks of ill-usage, was going home when he was suddenly knocked down by a heavy bl4w on the back of the head, delivered by the prisoner, who then jumped on him and kicked him. Witness was dazed when he succeeded in regaining his footing, but he told his wife to go for a policeman. She got the assistance of Constable Drew, who locked the prisoner up, and who told the magistrates that Cunning- ham was very drunk and very abusive. Prisoner said that he did not remember anything that had taken place, but Alderman Sutton, who was in the chair, told him that such conduct as his could not be tolerated. He would have to go to prison for a month for the drunken- ness, and for assaulting Bradshaw he would have to serve an additional term of two months' imprisonment. WARRINGTON TOPERS AND TEE TEMPERANCE PLEDGE. Two men who may be called "seasoned" topers made their appearance before the Warrington magistrates, on Monday. "They had been there before, many a time," and the probability is that they will be there again many a time, if their conduct in the past may be accepted as any indication of what it will be in the future. Both had very significant character sheets, of unenviable bulk, and both seemed to have made attempts at re- form, but without success. Daniel Crosby was the first to enter the dock, the charge against him being that, on Saturday night, he was drunkand disorderly in Scotland- road. He admitted the offence, and the Mayor, after inspecting his character sheet, asked what he meant by taking the pledge so often and not keeping it? He should take the pledge again and then ask Mr. Hunt to give him the character sheet and have it framed. It was his 65th appearance.—The Chief Constable: He once kept the pledge for six months, I believe; I don't know whether he was in goal during that period. (Laughter.)—Defendant: It is seven months since I was here.—The Mayor: The police have not been watching you carefully enough, perhaps. Defendant said he was keeping the pledge nicely when his brother happened to drop on him and they had a drink together.—The Mayor: You will be fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days' hard labour.—The next prisoner was John Behan, whose character was even worse than that of Crosby. He was charged with having been drunk and disorderly on Town-hill on Satur day night.—The Mayor: This is your 95th appearance here. You have been three years in prison, and have paid £2l in fines.—Defendant : I will try to be a teeto- taler.—The Magistrates' Clerk: How many times have you signed,John ?—Defendant : I havesigneda few times and I kept it twelve months. I will try again if you will forgive me this time,—The Chief Constable : It seems rather strange that men of the defendant's class come up most frequently in very cold weather and very hot weather. I suppose they want a stimulant.—Alder- man Harrison: The stimulants would not be of much consequence if people did make themselves a nuisance to others.—A fine of 10s. and costs was inflicted in this ease also.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Franeomb) and Alderman Sutton. _ _ .

DRUNKENNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—Charles Fowles, in Ellesmere-st., on Saturday, fined ss. and costs; James Henry Smith, in Buttermarket-et., on Saturday, fined ss. and costs; Henry Anderson, in Florsemarket-st., on Soturday, fined ss. and costs; Patrick Murray, in Buttersiarket-st., on Saturday, fined ss. and costs; and George Williams, in Enutsford-rd., on Saturday, 'fined 10s. and costs. DISORDERLY CONDUCT.—Charles Parry and Hannah Molyneaux, for having been guilty of disorderly conduct in Orford-lane, were each ordered to pay costs, 3s. 6d. Onsrauczzon.—Andrew Campbell was ordered to pay 2s. 6d., fur causing an obstruction in Sankey-et., on the sth inst., by allowing abandcart to remain there an un- reascnable length of time. CHIMNEY ON Fns.—George Tennant, for having allowed the chimney of his house to be on fire, on the 13th ult., was fined one shilling. TIIESDAY.—Before Messrs. W. Owen and E. M. Crosfield. ST. HELENS RECS. " A"' V. WIDNES ST. MAEY'S.—This match was played at City-road St. Helens, on Saturday before a moderate attendance The Recs. "A" team was composed of only 14 players. The game ended in a win for Widnes St. Mary's by 2 tries and 4 minors to 2 minors.

RUNCORN TRUE BLUES V. RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH.— This match was played on the ground of the former, and after an exciting game resulted in a win for the Blues by 1 try and 6 minors to Church 5 minors. Johnson scored for the Blues, Hill failing to notch the major point. RUNCORN HORNETS T. HALTON LIBERAL INSTITUTE.— This match was played on the ground of the latter, on Saturday, in fine weather. Result. Hornets, 2 goals and 3 minors; Institute, 1 minor: the Hornets' backs play&l a splendid passing game, Hillidge, Johnson, and Percival being the pick. WIDNES V. MANCHESTER RANGERS.—This match was played at Widnes on Saturday, before a large number of spectators. Kiddie, Stubbs, Holt, and Clarke, being absent, the home team was considerably weakened, and much indignation was expressed at Clarke having joined Runcorn. The visitors won the toss, and Farrell kicked off. Play settled in neutral territory, when from ' a scrimmage Hammett got possession, and crossed the line. The attempt at goal was, however, fruitless. From the drop out the the visitors were compelled to touch down. Farrell now began to assume something like his old form, and his tacklinr, proved safe and sure. A little combined play between tackling and Plumpton resulted in the ball being again kicked dead. The dash- ing and fast play of the visitors' forwards put the home backs on their merits, and the tackling was very credit- able. From a scrimmage in the visitors' quarters Far- rell passed to Brennan, and then to Plumpton. The latter making a splendid run, and grounded the leather amidst much cheering. The place kick was also taken by Plumpton, who landed a neat goal. Laws was next conspicuous with his forward play, and was within an ace of scoring. At half time the score was Widnes one goal and four minors to Manchester one try. On chang- ing ends the home team continued to have the best of the game, while the visitors seemed to strain every effort to equalize the score, and if possible to become victori- ous. The forward play of Laws, Wailing, Farmer, Pearson, and Gordon was ve:y effective, and as a result of their pressure another minor was added totheir score. The visitors in the second half occasionally visited the home quarters, but the backs proved too good for them. From a scrimmage in midfield Brennan secured, and with some dadgy play broke through the visitors' line, and grounded the ball. Plumpton again took the kick, but this time failed. Final result. Widnes one goal, one try, and five minors, to Manchester Rangers, one try, and one minor. The following represented the local team :—Hartles, back ; Plumpton, Brennan, Parkinson, and Farrell, three quarter backs; Drummond and How- ard, half backs ; Laws, Farmer, Wailing, Gandy, Smith, Gordon, Barber, and Pearson, forwards. Mr. Flowers was the referee. WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON.

The return match between these clubs took place at Warrington on Saturday, before three thousand spectators. The first match this season was interfered with by a dense fog, and only the first half was gone through, the match being finally abandoned. Since that time there has been a marked improvement in our local club's ranks, and their latest achievements over the renowned Swinton club seemed to give Saturday's match a foregone conclusion. In this opinion the least sanguine of the Warrington supporters agreed, but the fact had undoubtedly been lost sight of that Broughton had steadily advanced to the front, and were one of the most improved teams in the Manchester district. The War- ringtonians lacked the service of Nevins, but Broughton Broughton were placed at a further disadvantage, being without 7900 and flowers, their twe clever three- .

quartnea, In splendid football weather Frank Turner started tdwards the pavilion goal, with the sun in his eyes, Hassall's reply to the half-way flag was further improved by a smart rush of the Broughton forwards, a timely kick by Massey preventing further progress. Smart forward work by tile home front rank caused Broughton to defend, and some passing by Barnes, Antrobus, and Bate was cleverly frustrated by McArthur, who inter- cepted a pass to Lawless, and changed the venue to the half-way flag. However, Warrington once more returned to the attack, and Massey essayed a drop at goal, a minor following. Immediately on the drop out, Massey compelled another minor. Some smart passing by the home backs followed the drop out, and although Mc Dougall relieved, Tomlinson was at fault from a kick by Barnes, and the Broughton goal was again in jeopardy. Accurate tackling alone prevented Barnes from bringing about the downfall of the visiting goal, Wormald bring- ing his man down in the nick of time. Sumner here ' received from Whiteley, but he was at fault, and the certain chance of scoring which was presented to War- rington was not taken advantage of. The visitors were playing a determined game, and took advantage of many mistakes of the Warringtonians. A fine piece of work by McDougall was neutralized by Fair Turner, and Tomlinson luckily saved at a critical moment. A long kick by Massey sent the oval dead, and Donohue charging Smith's drop out, play was contested near the Broughton goal. The visiting forwards came to the rescue, and gradually rushed the leather to the half way flag, Bate coming in for notice with smart saves. A spell of give and take followed, the visitors playing a determined game, whilst the homesters were apparently taking matters easy. Aroused by the cheers of their anxious supporters, the " wirepullers " made a spurt, and a pretty exhibition between Antrobus, Fair Turner, and Barnes was the means of transferring the game to the Broughtcin end once more. The visitors would not be denied, and aided by the clever play •of Sumner and McDougall once more threatened danger'. Bandies judiciously kicked down the field, and another exhibition by the home backs was cleverly frustrated by Wormald who intercepted a pass to Barnes, and a lengthened series of scrimmages were witnessed near the Warrington goal. Repeated endeavours were made by the visiting halves to,cross the line, but the tackling was sure. A grand pass from Antrobus to Lawless relieved, and Tomlinson only managed to bring the Warringtonian down near the half way flag. Smith dribbled well, and the fine defensive play of Evans was of immense service to the homesters. Massey put in another huge kick, and half time was called.—War- rington four minors; Broughton nil. After the interval, Smith restarted, Bandies meeting the kick by punting in touch near the mid-way flag. From the line-out the oval fell Into the hands of McDougall, who rushed past the hree-qnarters at top speed. The responsibility was left to Evans, who made no mistake, and judging his man admirably he brought him down a yard from the the coveted line. Offside tackling by Broughton found play being contested at half way, and a kick by La- less further further improved the position of his side. Some good work by Donohue, the brothers Dillon, and Povey was neutralized by Hassan. Another piece of passing by Fair Turner, Barnes, and Lawless was neutralized by the latter failing to take the opening. Wormald here punted to Evans, who responded grandly, and time after tithe the Warrington custodian cleared his lines in surprising fashion. Antrobus foiled the opposing half backs, but his pass was not taken. The finest piece of work now took place in the match. Massey secureil from a pass from Bate, and kicking followed up he showed his opponents a clean pair of heels and got to within a few yards of the line, where Tomlinson was in waiting, but Massey had parted with the oval. Unfortunately, none of his comrades were at hand,and a certain chance of score- jug was lost. Immediately after Barnes had a shot at goal. the ball striking the posts. A series of exchange kicks followed, and Warrington were now displaying some- thing like their old form, but the effort was too late. Donohue and Bate repeatedly called forth cheers for their individual efforts, and Lawless put in a lofty kick over the line, and following up placed his men on side and Bandies dropped on the leather, but the point was not allowed. This decision certainly did not meet with the approval of the excited assemblage, and although Warrington pressed severely towards the close, they were unable to notch a tangible score, the final score reading—Warrington four minors, Broughton nil. Apparently Warrington held their opponents too lightly, there beings laxity of that dash•which had been the prevailing feature of the match the week previous. Evans played a capital game for Warrington back, never making the least semblance of a mistake. Coming nearer the pack, Bate's play was admirable, and he again proved what an admirable acquisition he has been to the team. Donohue was the -beat of the forwards, who

div.head: WELSH COLLIERY DISASTER.
div.p: THE WELSH COLLIERY DISASTER.
INQUEST ON THE VICTIMS.

The inquest arising from the disaster at the Llanerch Pit, Abersychan, Monmouthshire, through which 175 lives are now certified to have been lost, was formally opened, on Saturday, at the Town Hall, Pontypool, in the names of Joseph and Heary Howells, two of the deceased. A miner named Philip Williamson, who lost his son in the disaster, and but for an accident to his arm would have been employed in the colliery at the time of the explosion, insisted on coming into the room where the jury sat. He stated in an excited manner that he knew the cause of the accident, and if he was not heard he would write to the head authorities. Williamson accused the firemen who searched the mine I for traces of gas not doing their duty thoroughly. He was told that no evidence would be taken until the next sitting. After a brief discussion, the inquest was adjourned until the 25th instant..

div.head: RELIEF OF THE LkLSTRESSED.
div.p: RELIEF OF THE LkLSTRESSED.

The extent to which the disaster will affect the funds of the Monmouth and South Wales Miners' Provident Society is approximately estimated at about £30,000. To meet the expenses incidental to the funerals on Sun- day, the officials of the society, now at Abersychan, on Saturday. distributed £5 per head to the relatives of the deceased men who were members during life. At a meeting of the South Wales and Monmouth Colliery Sliding Scale Committee, on Saturday, at Cardiff, Sir W. T. Lewis presiding, £l,OOO was voted towards the provident fund, in meeting the claims which will be made upen it.

TELEGRAMS OF SYMPATHY. Further telegrams of sympathy and inquiry were re- ceived on Saturday. from her Majesty the Queen and the Home Secretary. The Queen's messages of condolence have been borne individually to the sorrowing widows and fathers and mothers. The latest details of the dis- aster were telegraphed to the Queen at Osborne, on Saturday, and again on Sunday.

div.head: NUMBER KILLED.
div.p: THE NUMBER KILLED.

The latest estimate gives the number killed as 175, though there were misgivings that even this is not the whole number, for inquiries are being received from all parts of the district, asking for information as to men who may have been working in the pit. No reply, of course, can be given to these, for the simple reason that the company have no accurate knowledge of who was underground at the time of the catastrophe, many con- tractcrs being employed in the mine, who themselves were killed with those who wGrked for them. Of the 175 deaths reported, the bodies of 167 have been brought to the bank, two cf the injured have died, and six men are known to be missing.

div.head: GRAPHIC ACCOUNT OF THE DISASTER.
div.p: GRAPHIC ACCOUNT OF THE DISASTER.

Mr. Joseph Morgan, the mine manager, who is praised on every hand, and whose devotion is the talk of the whole of the colliers of the district, has given a most graphic account of the disaster. "I was in the same seam," he said, "but not the same slope, in which the explosion occurred. I was in the very back of the work- ings when. I heard a dinning in my ears. It seemed as if some weight was pressing into them. Then we felt a rushing wave of air; it was travelling the wrong way, and we knew it was an explosion. I and the eleven men with me immediately started for the pit edge, but anxious as we were to get there, the horse we had with us was more so. Had he been human he could not have known better that something was wrong, and it was a desperate job to keep him back and from knocking us down. When we got to the bottom of the shaft we found three men unconscious. We dragged them to the fresh air, and then tried to signal to the top; but we found that the sage had been blown up. The men got me on their shoulders, and from there I climbed up the ropes till I got to the carriage. We then got another man up, and the two of us managed to get the carriage into the slides, and a nasty job it was, too, and when we had connected with the top I went up and reported, and then' returned down to get the saved up."

div.head: FUNERALS OF VICTIMS.
div.p: FUNERALS OF VICTIMS.

Monday was a day of morning at Pontypool and Aber- sychan, as the funerals of victims took place there. Thousands of visitors wearing mourning proceeded to the graveyard. The first part of the funeral procession, headed by the clergy and represeatatives of the colliery, left Abersychan at 12.30, and was followed by the rela- tives of the deceased. The long procession of coffins went fromAberyschan to Leinch-road, and there divided, 'part going to Trevethin, and part to Pontnewydd and Talywain Churchyards, The works were suspended at , the local collieries on Monday out of respect to the deceased, and the tradesmen's shops were closed. Many choirs from neighbouring churches arranged to sing at the interments. . . .

The second series of interments in connection with the Llanerch Colliery explosion took place on Tuesday, when there was again a long procession of coffins from Abersy- chan to the burial ground. There was again a large gathering of friends and sympathisers, though not so great as on Monday. There was not sufficient biers to carry coffins, which had to be carried shoulder high by the mourners in many cases. At present only about twenty of the 177 victims remain unburied.
EXPLORATIONS.

Exploring operations were carried on in the colliery all Tuesday; but up to night the searchers were unsuccessful in finding the body of the boy Lewis. Same days may elapse before that will be ac,comolished, as several falls have to be encountered and overcome.
ANOTHER DEATH.
William Tudgay, one of the men brought up injured from Llanerch pit on Thursday succumbed on Tuesday morning. His skull was fractured in the explosion, and he had along been in a precarious state.

div.head: CAPITAL AND LABOUR.
div.p: CAPITAL AND LABOUR.
• THE BLACKBURN COTTON TRADE.
The Bh;al;urn cotton trade is very depressed at the present time, and there are, it is estimated, fully 1,000 looms stopped, as well asa great quantity of prepazatory

machinery. THE STRIKE OF DUNDEE DOCKERS. The strike of Dundee dockers was ended on Monday, by the masters granting the demands of the men, who will now receive Bd. per hour. The masters also con- sent to employ extra hands in discharging jute ships, THE NORTHUMBERLAND MINERS.

A deputation of Northumberland miners waittd on the coalowners at Newcastle on Saturday to ask for a Maher advance in wages. The owners refused. but offered to reconsider the matter at the next ascertain- ment of prices for the quarter ending the 28th inst. THE MAVEN. The flatmen employed on the canal boats which are in the habit of coming to Liverpool have formed them- selves into a strong organisation, and branches of their union bavebeen formed all over Lancashire and Cheshire. Tile men are endeaeouring to have their hours of labour 'reduced.

div.head: lAHEASED WAGES IN THE MIDLANDS.
div.p: lAHEASED WAGES IN THE MIDLANDS.

The 'employers On the Z'oug.l7 ;;;17- trade in the Stafford and Worcester districts have conceded an advance of 10 per cent. in wages to the whole of the operatives, numbering about 4,000. The strike of brass foundry workers in the Rowley and Birming- ham districts has terminated, the masters having agreed to pay an advance ranging from 10 to 15 per cent. _ .

PROPOSED MINEOWNERS' FEDERATION. The adjourned meeting of colliery proprietors was held at Westminster, on Monday, to consider the pro- posed formation of a colliery proprietors' federation, and also the demand of the colliers for 10 per cent. advance in wages. It was unanimously resolved to re- sist the men's demand. A scheme for federation was then agreed to,with the exception of a few minor details, and the meeting adjourned for a week. REDUCTION .OF HOURS IN THE ALKALI TRADE.

It will be remembered that a few months ago the alkali workers of Northwich, Sandbach, and Wheelock obtained, by negotiation with Messrs. Brunner, Mond, and Co., Limited, a reduction of their hours of labour, by the alteration of theii working arrangements from two shifts of twelve hours each to theee shifts of eight hours each. The reduction of four hours was only accompanied by a very small reduction in wages. The salt workers in the Northwich, Sandbach, and Wheelock alkali trade, who were not inchtded in the arrangement, have now obtained from the directors of Messrs. Brun- ner, Mond, and Co. a similar reduction of working hours, and the new arrangements have come into oper- ation.

div.head: WAGES IN THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE.
div.p: WAGES IN THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE.

On Saturday night, a meeting ;Tcolliery surface men employed in the district was held at Wigan, for the purpose of considering what steps should be taken with regard to improving the wages paid to this class of workers. Mr. G. Woods, president of the Lancashire Miners Federation presided over a good attendance. It was stated that, though the price of coal had risen so much, and that advances of 30 per cent, had been con- ceeded to the miners, some of the men employed on the surface had only received 2d. or 3d. per day increase whilst others had received no advance at all. This was considered unsatisfactory, and it was contended that the wages of ethers employed about a colliery should be increased in the same ratio as the miners. The follow- ing resolution was passed :—" Considering the state of trade, and the unfair way in which we have been treated by our employers on the question, we, the surface men assembled in this meeting, agree to ask the Miner's Federation of Lancashire to give its consent to fourteen days' notice being given to terminate contracts unless 6cl. per day increase be given man and 3d. per day for every boy working about a colliery.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. FOOTBALL-RUGBY.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. FOOTBALL-RUGBY.
To-day's matches : Warrington v. Manchester Rangers at Manchester ; Rugcorn v. New Brighton at Runcorn; St. Helens v. Radcliffe at Radcliffe ; St. Helens Recs. v. Oldham at St. Helens.

Many people thought that Warrington had an easy thing on against Broughton on Saturday. The team that ran away with Swinton only the week before would not, it was thought, let Broughton have a look in on any account. But it turned out that there was a slight error in this calculation. The forwards who did so well againstthe renowned" Lions" from Swinton seemed to find it hard work to keep pace with the comparatively undistinguished Broughtoners. Instead of being always on the aggressive, the Warringtonians had a full share of the defensive play, and Evans, the full back, had a vast deal more to do than he had against Swinton. Evans, in fact, saved his side on two or three occasions, and again proved himself to be one of the best full backs in Lancashire.

Poor old St. Helens ! To go all the way to Kendal and return with the prodigious score of six tries and four minors to nil in favour of their opponents ! Surely there's something radically wrong, and needs remedying. Some of the supporters of the club attribute it to the repeated changes and trials in the composition of the team.

St. Helens Recreation fairly had an afternoon's " pic- nic " with Tottington. The latter seemed unable to do anything—in fact, they did little else besides gaze with surprise at the splendid rushes of the famous glass- works men. The fact that the score was no less than 5 goals, 3 tries, and 5 minors to nil, is the best evidence of the fact that Tottington were "never in it." Tot- tington, it was pretty plain, are not class enough for the Recs.

Lancashire turned out an indifferent team to meet Westmoreland at Wigan on Thursday such valuable men as Valentine, Flower, P. Steel, C. Anderton, and Haste- ham being absent, and the result was that the visitors were unexpectedly victorious. They deserved their success, and had all the best of the game until the last twenty minutes. Their passing was excellent, and their tackling fearlrss, that of their opponents being just as feeble. Both Armstrong and Robinson were seen to great advantage, at three-quarters. The Lancashire back division was weak, Marsh, Rumby, and Kendal alone doing well at times, whilst the forwards did not give satisfaction. Indeed the display all round was disap- pointing. Westmoreland had a distinct advantage in knowing each other's play, as they were almost wholly selected from two clubs. The result was a victory tor Westmoreland by a goal, two tries, and a minor to Lancashire two tries and two minors.

The teams were as follows :—Lancashire : W. Main. waring (Salford), full back ; W. Kendal (Askam), J. Marsh (Swinton), and W. Hastings, (Rochdale Hornets), three-quarter backs; J. Mills and W. Bumby (Swinton), halfbacks: W. Atkinson (Wigan), H. Eagles (Salford), C. Horley (Swinton), T. Melledew (Rochdale Hornets), T. Kent (Salford), Bullough (Wigan), J. Whittaker (Man- chester), Waugh (Rochdale St. Clements), and G. F. Wormald (Broughton) forwards. Westmoreland : W. G. Hogarth (Kendal) fullback; J. Armstrong (Kendal Hornets), J. Berry (Tyldesley and Kendal Hornets), and J. K. Robinson (Kirby Lonsdale),threequarter backs ; W. Ewans (Kendal) and W. Cross (Kendal Hornets), half backs :E. Wilson, R. Wiuskill, R. C. Beard (Kendal Hornets), G. Graham, R. Carradus, R. Moreton, R. Nicholson, J. Marshall,and P. Ireland (Kendal),, forwards. Referee : Mr. T. R. Sutton.

div.head: FOOTBALL-ASSOCIAT/ON.
div.p: FOOTBALL-ASSOCIAT/ON.

Haydock, at one period ef their career, used to be credited with being able to render a good account of themselves' in Cup ties, but alas the glotries ot the collier lads are departed. Recently in the JAucasiure Cup Burnley administered a "bitter pill" in the shape of a defeat of 15 goals to nit ; and last Saturday, Bootle repeated the dose to the extent of 11 goals to nil; in the contest for the Liverpool Cup. Surely Haydock's cup of sorrow has been drained to the dregs.

3I ISCELTAINEOVIS. Next Saturday the Warring ton Gymnasium team will meet an equal number of picked athletes from Bourne- mouth in the second round for the National Challenge Shield. The prospects of this encounter are in every way favourable for Warrington. In the first place the contost will take place at Warrington, and in the second place it is said that the Bournemouth team is a considerably less capable one than Exeter Hall, which Warrington':so handsomely defeated a week or two back. Another good augury for Warrington is that the same team which figured at Exeter Hall will in all likelihood be able to take the held again,

One ot the toughest encounters in the annals of chess is that now going on between the two great masters,Guns- berg and Tchigorin. At the cpening, ,of the match Tchigorin took the lead, but, Gunsberg began to display fine form and first drew level with and then went ahead of his opponent. The Russian, however, by fine play again got ahead, but the latest developement shows that the two players are again level, each having scored eight wins. The player that scores the first ten wins carries off the prize, and it is stated that the excitement at Havana, where the match is being played, is intense, opinions being equally divided as to the ultimate win- ner.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

THURSDAY.—nefore his Honour Judge Foulkes. THE CAUSE LIST comprised two default sum- monses, five adjourned plaints, 74 original plaints, and 37 judgment summonses. div.p: NEW WARRINGTON COMPANIES.

HENRY MILLING AND CO., LIMITED. This company has been registered with a capital of £20,000, divided into 2,00111 shares of £lO each. The objects for which the company has been established are to acquire and take over as a going concern the business now carried on in Horsomarket-st., and elsewhere, under the name of "Henry Milling and Company," to carry on this business as wholesale and retail grocers, tea and provision merchants, wholesale and retail chemists, &c. The first subscribers who take shares each are : Henry Milling, 3, Winmarleigh-st.; Jane Milling, 3, Winmar- leigh-st. ; John Walton, 29, Wilson Patten-st. ; Samuel George Davey, 9, Winmarleigh-st. ; William Horton, 21, River-rd., Latchford; Thomas Toft, 21, River-rd., Latchford; and Robert Lowe, 367, Knutsford-road, Latchford. The first three directors are Messrs. Henry Milling, John Walton, and Samuel George Davey. Mr. T. J. Ridgway is the solicitor to the company.

PETER STUBS, LIMITED. Peter Stubs (Limited) is registered with a capital of £150,000, in £lO shares. Object, to acquire and take over as a going concern, and afterwards carry on, the business now carried on by Peter Stubs at Warrington and Rotherham, mechanical engineer' boiler-maker,, iron master, colliery proprietor, iron and brass founder, coke manufacturer, metallurgist, and manufacturing chemist, or any of those trades or businesses. The first subscrib- ers (who take one share each) are :—P. Stubs, Warring- ton ; J. Marson, Hill Cliffe, Appleton, Cheshire; P. Stubs (the younger), Trinity College, Cambridge; F. A. Frost, Warrington ; T. Dwerryhouse, Moore, Cheshire; H. P. C. White, Penketh, Lancashire; E. W. Gaskell, Warring- ton. It need hardly be said that this new company starts with every prospect of succcess, taking over as it does a business which has gained so high a reputation in Warrington and district as that of Henry Milling and Co. It will be noted that some of the first subscribers for shares are employes of the firm. To-day, (Saturday), as will be seen from an advertisement in our columns, Messrs. Milling and Co. re-open the Warrington Cash Stores at 48, Sankey-et., with a new and selected stock of groceries, &c.
ST. JOHN'S CHURCH TEA. PARTY, WARRINGTON.

The agnual congregational tea party in connec- tion with St. John's Presbyterian Church, Winwick- st., was held on Thursday evening, in the school room. About 100 persons sat down to tea, the ladies who presided at the tables being Mesdames Long- din, Barlow, Sudlow, McLarty, Hawthorn, and McDowell, and Miss Gray. The chair at the subsequent proceedings was taken by the Mayor (Alderman Francomb),who was supported by Alder- man Sutton, the Rev. J. Warnock, the pastor, and leading members of the congregation. The Mayor ex- pressed pleasure at being amongst the friends at St. John's. It was the first occasion on which he had been with them, but he was quite certain that they were try- ing to carry out a good and useful work. These annual tea parties were looked upon with a very great amount of pleasure by every member of the congre- gation, more so by the younger than by the older ones. They also had the effect of bringing the members more closely together, so that they could exchange their thoughts, and talk about the work in their district. It also gave them an opportunity of hearing their clergyman speaking about what had been done in the past, and what it was intended to do in the future. He urged the young people to all become connected with the Sunday school, and pointed out that there was plenty of room for additional help in the way of teaching. The Rev. J. Warnock took the opportunity of thanking the members of the congregation, as well as outside friends, who had contributed to the renovation fund. The amount that had been spent in renovation was about £l3O, but that included other work besides the simple re-decoration of the inside of the building. Now that the church was looking so much better than it had done for a long time, he would like them to do something to justify the outlay made upon it. He was glad to say that of late the attendance at public wor- ship had considerably increased, but it was Still far from what they would like it to be. He hoped to see a still larger congregation in the future. A miscellaneous pro- gramme was then given, to which the following persons contributed :—Mrs. Sutton, Mrs. Shirlaw, Miss Field- house, Miss McLarty, Miss Dinwiddie, Mr. T. H. Long- din, Mr. Shakeshaft, Mr. Fieldhouse, Mr. C. H. Ward. and Master F. Jones. Mr. George Riley was the accom- panist.

THE CHARGE AGAINST A RUNCORN FOOTBALLER. EXTRAORDINARY EVIDENCE. William F. Hancock, a fitter in the employ of Runcorn Waterworks Company, and a well-known football player, was brought up at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, charged on remand with having feloniously assaulted Maria Barker, aged 19 years, daughter of Francis Barker, of the Ferry Inn, Ch urch-st.--Mr. F. A. Lake prosecuted, and Mr. Mul- holland (instructed by Mr. A. Linaker) defended the prisoner. Mr. A. Thomas was the magistrate. The prosecutrix stated that Mr. Bancroft occupied la shop adjoining her father' i house,and the prisoner lodged there. About half-past six on the evening of the 29th January, in consequence of what Mrs. Bancroft's little girl told her, she went into the shop, and Mrs. Bancroft asked her if she would stop and put the child to bed and wait until Fred had dressed himself and was ready to go out. The prisoner was washing himself in the kitchen. After Mrs. Bancroft had left, the prisoner locked the door, and went upstairs. He called to her and asked her to go upstairs, as he had something parti- cular to tell her, which he did not want the child to hear. After he had called several times she went upstairs. As soon as she got on the landing, the prisoner seized hold of her, carried her into his room, and committed the offence. She both" cried and screamed, and fought with all her might." Afterwards her mother was knocking at the door, which the prisoner opened, and they all went out together.—The witness was cross- examined at length by Mr. Mulholland, to show that she had been a consenting party. Witness denied that she had ever sat on his knee or kissed him, or that Mrs. Bancroft had ever remonstrated with her about her con- duct with the prisoner. She also denied other acts of familiarity which it was alleged have taken place. Mary Ann Barker, the mother, said on the night in question, about twelve minutes to seven, she was knock- ing at the door about two minutes before the prisoner opened the door. She walked in the shop, and asked her daughter if she were coming home. Thereupon they left the house together, the prisoner walking down the street. When they got home, her daughter made a com- plaint to her, and she put her to bed and sent for a doctor. Inspector Bowyer deposed to apprehending the pri- soner about ten ' o'clock, and charged him with the offence. He declared the charge was untrue, and made an unchaste suggestion with regard to the girl he was engaged to be married to.—Dr. McDougall gave the result of his medical examination, and expressed the opinion that the girl until the night of the assault was a Virgo intacto. Mr. Mulholland,in his address for the defence,asked his Worship if he could commit the prisoner for trial on the absolute and uncorroborated statement of the prosecutrix or any woman. Her evidence was not only ineorrobor- , ated, but was weakened and almost destroyed by her own admissions. He accused her of perjury, and said she had made up this story to meet her mother's reproba- tion. He called Joseph Bancroft, carter, of 89, Church-st., who said the prisoner had lodged with him since last September. For the past two or three months the prosecutrix had come daily into the house uninvited, and he had fre- quently seen lier sitting on the prisoner's knee, kissing. He had heard her dare the prisoner to kiss her and he had , done so.—By Mr. Lake : This has been done quite openly. There was no indelicacy. Mrs. Bancroft gave evidence to the same effect and , said she had told the prosecutrix not to joke with the I prisoner so much as it was not a right thing to do, be- cause he was to be married to another woman. On the night in question, witness was at the Co-operative tea party.—By Mr. bake : She had often asked the prose- cutrix to help her in the shop. Mary Fleyes, 14 years of age, who had been servant to the Bancrofts said she had frequently seen the prosecu- trix sit on the prisoner's knee, and had seen kissing. On the second January, Mrs. Bancroft was in Liverpool, and she was in charge of the house. At five o'clock, the prisonercame to his tea, and the prosecutrix followed him in and said she had" COMO to make Fred's tea." She did so, and then sat on his knee. Shortly aft-'- wards she asked witness to fetch the little girl home and she went out. On returning five minutes later, the front door was locked, and she knocked and rang the bell several times. , Then she heard footsteps descending the stairs, and the prosecutrix opened the door for her. Some time after- ' wards the prosecutrix asked her to go for the little girl ; again. She was away about five minutes, and when she , came back, the door was again fastened. She rang the bell, but got no answer, so she walked round to the back, and entered that way. She heard someone up- stairs, and the prisoner and prosecutrix walked down.— By Mr. Lake: There is a sitting room with a bed up- , stairs. She had seen albums in the room, and the pri- soner and prosecutrix said they had been looking at the . photographs. At this stage Mr, Mulholland asked if it was necessary to put the prisbner in the box, and his Worship replied in the negative. He shculd not send the case for trial. The prisoner was then discharged, and as he left the ' court he was received by a large crowd of people, j amongst whom women-kind predorninated. Ran ock was married to "the girl of his choice" on Tuesday.
