MR. T. H. PEARSON AND MR. J. W. EMMETT. Sir,—At the last meeting of the Newton Improvement Commissioners, Mr. Emmett, the chairman, is reported to have said that I made certain statements respecting him to Sir Richard Moon, an 4 that I commissioned another to do so. Mr. Emmett's statements are absolutely false. I may Say that I sent a copy of the paper containing the report to Sir Richard Moon, and I have a letter from him deny- ing Mr. Emmett's statements. The public will judge for themselves as to the pro- priety of the language used by Mr. Emmett,who, though Chairman of a public body, left the business of the meet- ing to make baseless charges against one who was not present to deny them,—l am, dear sir, yours faithfully, THOMAS H. PEARSON. Redclyffe, Newton-le-Willows, 13th Feb., 1890.

div.head: TILE YEOMANRY.-AN INJUSTICE TO FARMERS.
div.p: TILE YEOMANRY.-AN INJUSTICE TO FARMERS.

Sir,—lt was the proud boast of one of England's poets that slaves could not breathe in England, but lam inclined to think could the said poet have known how some of the landlords of this country treat their tenantry, it would ve-y much have moe' fled his

views. In the fel:dal times we read tkat lands were held by the tenantry on the condition that they provided certain horses and men in time of war, but in these latter days the landlords, or at all events some of the Cheshire land- lords, demand in rent the full value of tile land, and require the tenant to serve or pros de a man, or man and horse, for the yeomanry in addition. Can you conceive this possible now that the farmer has so much to com- pete against? Whether he can afford or not, whether wanted at home or not, the Cheshire landlord insists upon his leaving home for a certain number of days in the year, and providing a horse, to do duty as soldier in order to plea,e the vanity or maintain the dignity of his landlord. Many a mother has had occasion to grieve fa a son gone astray through the bad influence of the system, and many a father or son who hated soldiering, as they hate poison,have been forced to take up arms and don a uniform, because it pleased a landlord to require it. Yet in spite of objections of all descriptions the mandate still goes forth—" Unless you do this you can- not have the farm." It is an abuse that is not much talked about, because the farmer feels his dependence, and he is afraid to speak. Further. the horse useable as a charger is often of no other use whatever, and to com- pel him to waste his time and spend his money against his inclination is altogether at variance with the spirit of the laws of this country, and it will be a boon to the many farmers • when some enlightened legislator gets it altered.—Yourstruly,
SEN EX X.

OUR NATIONAL POVERTY, AND GOVERNMENT EXTRAVAGANCE. Sir,—l am sorry that I should forward a mis-statement respecting the age of Benjamin Stewart West. The error was not mine; the statement I forwarded to you I copied from a contemporary, whose information may have been incorrect in the matter of age. At all events, his periods of service should have entitled him to a more liberal pension. His case is similar in many respects to hundreds of others, showing the neglect and indiffer- ence on the part of the Government to the dezdinin7, years of men who have risked life, and sacrificed health on the altar of duty, and for what? For the independ- ence and honour of their country in every clime, for a country which, while these men were radergoing untold and incredible hardships in her cause, could not supply with ordinary comforts and sufficient food. Those who survive the rush of battle, the effects of climate, the want of food, and lack of medicine when ill or wounded, and are not strangled by red tape may succeed in get- ting a shilling a day after 21 years' hard see vice. Not only the men who have served their country as soldiers and sailors—men of war—are subject to want and starvation, in the decline of life, or old age. But, many of those who serve their country in the arts of peace, steadily, soberly, honestly, are even worse off. They have no pension, and after a long life of toil with unblemished character they have the Workhouse or the grave to go into. The latter in many cases preferable. Mr. Winterbotham, speaking at Dewsbmy a few days ago, gave utterance to some remarkable statements with regard to our national poverty and our national wealda. He quoted a remark by Carlyle "that there were plenty of shirts in the world and plenty of bare backs, but the problem was how to bring the shirts and bare backs together." He mentioned that the realized wealth of the country was £9,410,000,000, or about £270 per head of the population ; the yearly income of Eng- land £1,200,000,000, or £5 a week per family; the sav- ings of the country were variously estimated at from £.300,000,000 to £400,000,000, and yet with all this wealth " the people starved in the midst of plenty that in London one sixth of the people died paupers, and that in twelve of the largest cities of our country 75 per cent. of those who passed 70 years of age died in the Workhouse. "This is a state of things," says Mr. Winterbotham, " with which I for one am not content," I endorse that discontent. Some people will tell you that such a state of things is the result of the operation of natural laws. Natural rub- bish! yes rubbish of the most rotten character. It is brought about in a great measure by laws made by a dominant class for their own benefit—the drink laws and the land laws exercising a mighty influence in the matter. I have referred to the poor soldier pensioner with his shilling a day, and that there was, and is a class of honest sober people who work when they can— but who, when they work, do not get sufficient for pre- sent wants, to say nothing of providing for the future, and who, wken strength fails—well in many cases starve. As a case in point, short opera cloaks, made of plush and silk, quilted throughout, costing a guinea, are given out to be made to a middle woman, at is. qd. each, the plush and silk being found, but the middle woman find- ing wadding, stiffening for the belt, hooks and eyes, and cotton. Those skilled workers who work for this woman can only get wretched wages. Miss Black, who made this statement, says that many of these skillel workers spend the winter in the workhouse! She her- self had a long cloak made for which she paid 12s. 6d. for the making, hanging sleeves, fur edging, and quilted throughout. The mantle maker getting such a cloak to make from the shop would only get is. 6d. I Is there nothing wrong here? And yet we are told you must not interfere with " freedom of contract." Why not ? If one of the contracting parties is robbed by the other, it is surely the duty of some one to step in and do justice. Our Government is too busy just now in squandering English money in providing for Irish landlords, many of whom have been life long robbers. Mr. Winterbotham's remedy for this state of things is education. So say I. Not so much the three Ws as political education, the three R's as a stepping stone to the study of the political history of the past, the political aspect of the present. Looking at these calmly and dispassionately, what is the outlook for the future? If there is no brighter pros- pect than legislation framed by a Tory Government, backed by sham Liberals, the outlook is gloomy, dark, and uncertain, but we hope for better things—things attainable if well striven for, things worth having and to be had by intelligent combination and determination, that the sum of human rights shall be equally shared, and that no wrong be done to eithcr employer or en:- ployed.—l am sir, yours truly, CYMRO.. Blakey Bridgcs, Feb., 12, lea

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
HALY-YEARLY MEETING OF THE COMPANY.

The ninth ordinary general meeting of the Manchester Ship Canal Company was held in the Gentlemen's Con- cert Hall, Manchester, on Thursday at noon. Sir J. C. Lee presided; and there was a large attendance of shareholders. The Chairman read a letter from Lord Egerton of Tatton, who is confined to his room by an intermittent fever, expressing regret at his absence, he having just returned from the South of France in order to attend the meeting. His lordship had, however, sent a 'letter describing the progress of the canal during the last half-year, which was read. Lord Egerton con- cluded his statement with a reference to the death of Mr. Daniel Adamson and Mr. Walker, the contractor. The report, which had already been published, was taken as read. The Chairman, in moving its adoption, referred to the financial position of the undertaking, and in this connection stated that, including the profit from the Bridgewater Canal, which was tied up until the contract was completed, the shareholders had before them capital to the amount of £4,000,000. That, he thought, quite disposed of the rumours which had been circulated by their opponents that they were getting short of capital. It would be necessary for thew, to call up another pound, making in all V, on the Ist June. He was glad to be able to report that the last call, due on the 24th of last month, had been paid. There were hardly any arrears. (Applause.) That was a very satisfactory state of affairs, and it showed the great interest that was being taken in the great undertaking. (Applause.) The Chairman then referred to the progress of the works, and begged to move the adoption of the report. —Mr. J. K. Bythell seconded the resolution. The more they looked into the matter the more the directors were convinced that the necessary traffic would be obtained, and that even at the opening there would 'be a quantity of traffic which would amaze them. Mr. James Johnstone said he would like to make one sugges- tion. He would like to suggest most respectfully that the docks of Manchester, or some part of this great work, ' should be called after Daniel Adamson. (Applause.) The Chairman promised that the valuable suggestions of Mr. Johnston and Mr. Roby should have the consider- ation of the directors.—The motion was adopted.—Sir J. C. Lee, Mr. A lex . Henderson, Mr. Joseph Leigh, and Mr. S. R. Platt were re-elected directors of the company. —A vote of thanks to the directors concluded the pro- ceedings of the ordinary meeting.—The meeting then , became special, when sanction was given to the directors to proceed with two bills in Parliament—one for making alterations at the estuary, and ,for makiug wharves, warehouses, &c. The meeting closed witla a vote of thanks to chairman and directors. DIVERSION OF THE IRWELL.

During the past few weeks the Irwell has been diverted on the west side of Stickin's Island, and also at Hulme's Bridge. The old lock house at the latter place has been demolished, the locks have been swept away, and the footbridge which spanned the river has dis- appeared. Communication between Flixton and Lower Irlarn has been maintained by the construction of a tem- porary footbridge across the new cutting of the river in the meadows at Boysnope. The canal is now being cut at various points where the waters of the Irwell formerly ran, and the cuttings between Lower Irlam and Barton Bridge have,with one exception, been connected. Rapid progress is being made with the construction of the docks and sluic,Ps at Salteye. Men are working night and day at the cutting between Barton Bridge and the aqueduct, so that the Irwell may be again diverted and the foundations of the new bridges proceeded with.

div.head: MISSION AT ACTON GRANGE.
div.p: MISSION AT ACTON GRANGE.

During the past three weeks Mr. John Watson, mis- sianaly of Runcorn, has been c m ionductin special mission services on the Acton Grange section. °The attendance kas been good and deep interest had been taken in the mission. Especially was this the case at Stockton Heath where a good work was done. In connection with the special mission, at Acton Grange, a bible reading was given by Miss Dutton, of Moore, on Thursday afternoon to the women, Mrs. Golightly taking part. Several women from the huts attended.

ACCIDENT AT TFIELWALL. On Monday afternoon, a young man, named A,frod Cox, who is employed on the Thelwall section of the Ship Canal, met with an accident whilst at work. When in the act of getting on to a moving locomotive he stumbled and the succeeding wagon ran over his foot, it being so badly crushed that probably amputation will have to be resorted to. .

div.head: FLOODS.
div.p: THE FLOODS.

The damage occasioned by the recent flooding of the Ship Canal at Thelwall, has to a great extent been recti- fied. Many of the railway lines have had ta be repaired, and in many instances almost reconstructed. All the water has not yet been got out of the cutting, but in its present state it offers no impediment to the progress of the general work in the vicinity of the locks. Many repairs have had to be done consequent upon the floods, which have been the means of delaying the ordinary work for several days.

ALARMING EPIDEMIC OF INFLUENZA. AT ST. HELENS. An epidemic of influenza recently broke out in St. Helens and has spread with alarming rapidity among all classes of the population. Messrs. 11. and F. Knowles, surgeons to the large glass making firm of Pilkington Bros., give the approximate number of patients under their care as between 200 and 300. The medical officer of health (Dr. M'Nicoll) and his assistant (Dr. Dale) have their hands full of cases. Dr. E. Casey, of Sutton, has nearly seventy cases in that district, and all other medical gentlemen are having a busy time. Many of the cases appear to have assumed an acute form, there being such complications as congestion of the lungs with inflammation of the bowels. THE INFLUENZA AT EARLthOWN. The epidemic of influenza at Earlestown and Newton continues to afflict a large number of people of all ages. As stated in our last issue the various works in the neighbourhood are inconveni- enced by the extremely large number of absentees through the complaint, while the attendance of children at the schools is much less than it has been for a long time past.

div.head: PARNELL COMMISSION. JUDGES' REPORT.
div.p: PARNELL COMMISSION. JUDGES' REPORT.

The report of the Parnell Commission was issued on Thursday night, and is a voluminous document. The Commissioners find that the respondents did not conspire to bring about the independence of Ireland, though seven of them and Mr. Davitt established and joined; in the Land League organisation with that object in view. The charge that the respondents denounced certain crimes in public and afterwards led their sup- porters to believe that such denunciations were not sincere, is found to be not establishcd, and Mr. Parnell is acquitted of the charge of insin- cerity in denouncing the Phoenix Park murders, ' the letter on which this charge was based being declared a forgery. The Commissioners find that the respondents did not directly incite to crime other than intimidation, and it is not found peoved that they made payments to incite to crime. Three specific charges against Mr. Parnell are found not proved, one of these being in reference to the Kilmainham negotiations, and the others in refer- ence to his alleged intimacy with the Invincibles, and his alleged remittances of money to aid the escape of F. Byrne.

PENKETH. THE INFLUENZA AT PF.NRETII. The influenza has at last reached Penketh, and it is said that there are a number of cases of a Russian character. The epidemic is spreading and getting fresh victims every day. MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.

On Wednesday evening Mr. Thomas Bell read an interesting essay on "Trees." A description of the construction, uses, and localities of different trees, British and foreign, was given in a very clear and satisfactory manner. There as a fair attendance of members.

CAPTURE OF A Fox AT BOLD. On Tuesday, as Mr. W. Robinson, agent for Bold Hall estate, and the keepers, were out ferreting for rabbits, they came across a tine vixen fox, in a large burrow. Mr. Robinson despatched one of the keepers for tools to unearth the animal, and its life was quickly disposed ot. The affair caused quite a stir in the neighbourhood. It seems that there is another fox prowling abut, and means are being taken for its capture. PLOUGHING AT BOLD.

On Thursday the farmers of the district of Sankey and Bold gave what is called "a helping day" for Mr. W. lloward, who has gone to live at Barrow Hall. There was a fair number of teams present, and each teamster did his best. Mr. Barker, cham- pion ploughman, was also present on behalf of Messrs. Ransome and Sons, implement manufac- turers, and worked one of their latest ploughs. Mr. Howard provided an excellent dinner at the close, and a very pleasant evening was spent.

div.head: DRIII.I AND FIFE BAND CONCERT.
div.p: DRIII.I AND FIFE BAND CONCERT.

A concert in aid of the fund of this hand was given in the Penketh Wesleyan schoolroom, on last evening week. Mr. C. E. Parker presided and there was a good attendance. Mr. W. G. Read, of Liver- pool, the " Concertina King," and also Master G. Read, aged 5 years,the smallest concertina soloist in the world, were present, and. daring the evening

Mr. Read gave several selections, amongst which were an imitation of a full military brass band with trombone solo, operatic airs on two instruments, and also imitation of a church organ. Master G. Read played- "The Last Rose ot Summer" and " The Bohemian Girl," which were given in a man- ner that caused much applause. Mr. Frederick Sandall, played a selection on his fairy bells, and Miss Lang,don, of Liverpool, who was staying in the neighbourhood, was asked to sing, and she will- ingly responded to the call. The band played vari- ous selections, and other ladies and gentlemen took part. Mr. D. Garnett said if they remained still in debt after the concert he would give one half the debt, if someone else would give the other half. Upon this, the Chairman said he would give the other half. The concert was a success financially and otherwise.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 15, 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 15, 1890.

John Flood, a boy, said Mrs. Keating was his mother. On the 24th January he was sent with his stepfather's supper to the Atlas Works. He got there about half-past seven and found his father in the hut sitting on a bench. He said he was gassed, and felt bad with a pain in his head. Witness left the supper and went for his mother. Deceased said he would be home after him. His mother and Mrs. Allen afterwards went to the hut. The de- ceased did not appear drunk. His father had been gassed before many a time, and he usually took a glass of ruin to cure him. His mother did not give him a glass of rum or anything. Witness was left with the deceased. and remained with him for two hours. During that time, the deceased did not speak a word. When he got home he told his mother the deceased did not seem so bad.—By Inspector Keighley : His mother had never said " Johnny, you must not tell that father was drunk and that we put him in the hut, or we shall not get any club money." _ . _ _ _

Alice Keating„ the widow of the deceased, said he was about 49 years of age. He was a chemical labourer, and lived at 7 Marsh-street. On Friday night, the 24th January, her son brought word that, his father was bad, and she and Mrs. Allen went to a hut in the yard. She asked him what was the matter, and he replied "Nothing, only I got a bit of gas all day." He was coughing, and "didn't complain of nothing at all." She told the lad to stop with his father. She had got no money, or she would have got some rutia.—The Coroner: Do you think it was right to leave him in that hut.— Witness said hewas not bad at all ; he was as well as ever she had seem him in his health.—The Coroner : And you wish the jury to believe that.—Witness : It's the truth. He said he would be home soon.—Witness, continuing, said she had never seen the deceased since the Tuesday previous. When the lad came home, he said the deceased had fallen asleep on the bench. He had not much money for drink, he had too many to keep.—ln answer to Inspector Keighley, she denied that she had ever said she and another woman found the deceased at the bottom of the steps and laid him oa a form in the hut.—By the Coroner : She seemed to think he had drink. As she was sworn like that, he might have been more sober.—ln reply to Mr. Keighley witness denied that her husband was in any club.—Mr. Cook said the woman came to him for club money on Saturday morning.—The woman prostested that her evidence was the truth.—The Coroner said either she or some of the other witnesses were telling falsehoods. Mrs. Allen (recalled) said if Mrs. Keating said her husband never looked better in his life, the statement was not true. He looked very bad.—Mrs. Keegan, wife o:Lawrerce Keegan, of 6 Marsh-street, said Mrs. Keat- ing had told her she was frightened about the club money, as she had found her husband at the bottom of the seeps in the yard, and he was drunk. Dr. Plutchinson said he examined the man at the works. He was unconscious, and paralysed on the left side. He examined his head and found a very extensive bruise on the right side of the head, also a small incised wound on the top of the head towards the left side. It was half an inch long and penetrated to the bone. There was also a bruise on the left side of the head. He was taken to the Hospital, but never regained consciousness, and died on Saturday, the first February. He had made a post mortem examination, and discovered a fracture of the skull four and a half inches in length. There was an extensive blood clot between the skull and the brain on both the right and left sides of the head. The cause of death was the pressure of these blood clots on the brain, and the fracture had been caused by violence.— By Inspector Keighley : Some of the injuries might have been caused by a fall down the steps. He must have had more than a blow to cause the injuries.—By the Coroner : In his opinion the man could not have spoken to his wife and son suffering from a fracture of the skull. There was blood on the hair of the man. After receiv- ing those injuries he did not think it possible for the man to walk into the hut ; he must have been carried in.—By Mr. Cook : There were no indications that the man had been gassed. William Melton, plumber, deposed to finding the deceased in the hut about seven o'clock on Saturday morning. He was lying on the floor. He was as cold as ice. The hut was in the same condition it was on the previous night. Witness at once informed the time- keeper and the man was taken to the Hospital.—Mr. Cook said the deceased finished work at half-past five, and he had no right in the works on the night in ques- tion. .

The Coroner said the evidence of the wiflow, Mrs. Allen, and the boy.was worthless, and he was of opinion that it had been trumped up to hoodwink the jury. He should disallow their expenses. There was no evidence to show how this man received his terrible injuries, and he suggested that an open verdict be returned so that the police might prosecute their inquiries, and if they discovered that anyone was to blame bring them before the proper tribunal.—The jury returned the verdict suggested.

WARRINGTON PEERS' " ECONOMIC " BUILDING SOCIETY. The first annual meeting of the First Warrington Peers' " Economic" Building Society, was held at the offices, King-st., on Thursday evening. There was a good attendance of members. The President (Mr. T. Birchall) presided, and the other directors present were Messrs. J. Albinson, T. G. Hulse, A. Rath bone, J. Smethurst, and S. Taylor; W. Walker (secretary), H. J. Longton (solicitor), and T. Roberts (members' auditor). The CHAIRMAN said their society had now been in existence about a year, and he thought the amount of progress they had made was fairly gratifying. When they considered the number of similar societies in War- rington, all catering for members, and all trying:to do the best they could, he thought they had made very satisfactory progress. (Hear, hear.) It seemed to him that they had been very much in the condition of a young couple just setting up housekeeping, who, haying made up their minds to get married, had to furnish their house. During the past year they had been furnishing their house. They tried ons house, but it was not quite convenient enough, but their worthy secretary had now got into quarters which were much more convenient for all their operations. There was one thing he wanted par- ticularly to impress upon them, and that was the desira- bility of extending amongst their friends membership of the society. Of course the larger their society got, the oftener they could have their ballots. They had never in...de great pushes in order to make a great show of balloting, and, therefore, he did not think they had followed the example of some other societies. He might tell them that next week they would be able to satisfy every claim that had been made upon them by ballot. He saw that another very prominent society in the town, that had its meeting five or six weeks ago, after three years existence had had sixteen ballots, but he found that only eleven had been paid up, five being still unpaid. That, as they knew, was balloting a long way in advance. But what advantage was it to the members to have a ballot when they could not be paid for a year or two hence ? What they wanted was that their society should move steadily ahead, so that when they engaged in a ballot they should have some chance of providing the money for those who got it. The directors had tried to work the society with the greatest economy, and they had passed a special resolution declining to take all the remuneration the rules allowed them, only taking one half. (Hear, hear.) They would notice from the balance sheet that out of their year's working they were able to give a bonus of Sixpence per share, and this six- pence amounted to nearly 2i per cent, on the investment, which, considering all the costs they had had to go through, was a very gratifying result. (Applause.) THE DIRECTORS' REPORT. The following was the report of the directors :—" The Directors herewith submit the result of the first year's : working of the Society. After writing off a reasonable amount of the formation and other expenses there remains a balance of profit of £25 7s. 51-d., which will doubtless be considered very satisfactory for tDe first year, and the directors recommend that a bonus of six- pence per share be given on all paid up shares, and the balance carried to the reserve fund. They wish also to urge upon every member the desirability of bringing the advantages of the Society under the notice of their friends with a view to making up the full membership, which would be the means of raising the society's income, and thereby securing greater advantages by more frequent ballots and increased profits. The follow- ing directors retire this year, but are'eligible for re-elec- tion, viz. :—Messrs. Thomas Birchall, James Smethurst, Samuel Jones, and Samuel Taylor. The Auditor, Mr. Thomas Roberts. also retires, but is eligible for re-elec. tion."—Mr. R. DoweLt, in moving the adoption of the report and balance sheet, said he thought the report a very satisfactory one for a first year's working. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. LAKE seconded, and after a few remarks by Mr. LONGTON, in which he referred to the encouraging prospects of the Society, the report was adopted unani- mously.

div.head: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES _ 4T RUNCORN. •
div.p: UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES _ 4T RUNCORN. •

RAIN. The third of the present series of lectures on phy- siography, was given, in Bethesda Lecture Hall, on Tuesday evening, when Mr. Mackinder, M.A., dea t with the subject of " Rain." There was again a good audience and the lecture was illustrated by mesns of a oxyhydrogen lantern,manipulated by Mr. H. W. Handley. At the outset the Lecturer spoke of the relation between water and air, and by describing a few simple experiments which the audience could perform for themselves, demonstrated that water was always present in the atmosphere. There were two methods by which water passed into the air as invisible gas ; there was the process of evaporation and of ebbulition. There was anot'ier state when liquid water hung suspended in the air, end was visible as dust—as cloud. There was a certain distinct quantity of water which the air could take up ; and it could not take any more. On a windy day, pools made by rain would dry up very much faster than on another day, simply because the air which came down drank its fill, and quickly passed on whilst drier air was carried on and took up the remainder of the,water. Hot air could drink more water than cold air. There was a certain distinct quantity of water which air could drink up, Suppose he increased the temperature from 30 degrees to 31, perhaps he should increase the power of air to hold water to the extent of one grain, but supposing the air had a temperature of 70 degrees and he increased the temperature to 71 ; then he should find that he had increased the power of the air to hold water not by one grain, but by five. In other words in cold wintry weather the air contained vastly smaller moisture than in hot summer weather which was a result one would hardly have expected, because the air in winter was much damper than the air in hot summer weather. They came to the extraordinary paradox, that dry air might contain more water than moist air, and that actually wet air might have less water in it than dry air. The capacity of hot air was vast; the capacity of cold air was small. Chill hot air,and it would throw down no dew, no cloud, because, although it contaiaed a large quantity of water, it was not satur- ated. Other and colder air, if it only contained one half the quantity of water, but was saturated, chill it ever so little, and down fell water. So in winter the air was constantly throwing down a little water. We did not get thunder showers, but we got a constant drizzle. Th• Lecturer went on to describehow in some parts of the world, the air was hot and intensely thirsty and would lick up the last drop of water. The rivers from the mountains never found their way to the sea ' • they grew smaller and smaller and ended in a marsh. Rivers larger than the Mersey were drunk up by the wind. So it was in the heart of Africa and of Asia and even in some parts of America and even Australia. In Eng- land the prevalent winds were south west, and hav- ing come from warmer and ocean regions, were laden with water, and the moment they got chilled, they threw down moisture, and hence our land was not a desert. (Applause.) ENGLISH SOCIAL REFORMERS.

At the conclusion of the lecture, Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys read the report of Mr. A. Hassall, M.A., student and tutor of Christ Church College who was the examiner at the examination on 4. English Social Reformers," which has already been published. The report of the lecturer, the Rev. W. Hudson Shaw, M.A., was also read. Runcorn Centre, he said, must be regarded as more than satisfactory. Success, he added, was chiefly owing to the admirable manner in which the lectures had been organised by a representative Committee and the hardworking, enthusiastic secretary, Mr. Wynne Humphreys.—Mr. Mac Kinder then presented the certifi- cates to the successful students whose names are ap- pended :—Passed with distinction : Ist (and prize) J. E. Clay-den ; 2nd, H. Head ; satisfied the examiner, M. E. Benbow, C. Ditchtield, M. E. Naylor, J. Shingler, A. M. Taylor.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY DEATH AT WIDNES.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY DEATH AT WIDNES.

CLUB MONEY, AND CONTRADICTORY EVIDENCE. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, on Tues- day afternoon held an inquest, at Widnes Accident Hospital, 00 the body of John Keating, a Chemical labourer, who died in that Institution, on Saturday. under the circumstances detailed below. Mr. Cook was present on behalf of the Atlas Chemical Works, and Superintendent Johnston and Inspector Keigh- ley acted on behalf of the police. Adam Green, of West-st., said about five o'clock on Friday, the 24th January last, he went to his work. He was in charge of the chambers and the gas. At that time he saw the deceased in the yard. At half past seven he went home to his supper along the West Bank rail- way and he saw the deceased walking towards the works. He was staggering from one side to another. The deceased was drunk, and stumbled against a waggon which was in motion, but he did not fall. About ten minutes past eight he saw Mrs. Keating and another woman come from the lime hut, and about 12 o'clock lie entered the hut, and found Keating lying asleep on the floor with " paper leggings" for a pillow. About 540 in the morning, Keating was still lying in the same posi- tion. He attempted to rouse Keating, and told him that he was going to open a chamber, and he must clear out of that hut. The deceased did not make a move. He knew the deceased had slept in that hut for four nights during that week.—By the Coroner: Deceased was not hurt by striking against the waggon. He had never seen a man " gased " with chlorine gas in his life—By Inspector Keighley : The deceased would have to climb a wall five feet six inches high to get to the hut.—By Mr. Cook: There was no gas escaping from the chambers that night: When men were in drink they often excused themselves to the foremen by saying Oh, its gas, not drink." The deceased was not working that night. Martha Allen, wife of Hugh Allen, 34 Cromwell-st., deposed that at a quarter past seven on Friday wilt, the 24th January, she met Mrs. Keating in West-st. Mrs. Keating said her son brought word that her husband was bad at the hut in the yard. She went with Mrs. Keating to the hut and found the deceased sitting on a bench. He said he was gassed, and his head felt bad. TheT stopped a few minutes, and then laid him on his left side on the bench. Afterwards they left him. If Mrs. Keating had said they found him at the bottom of the steps it was not true. She did not notice whether the man had had drink or not, but the place smelled of gas. She could not say whether he was drunk or not. She had never heard Mrs. Keating threaten her son that they must not tell where they found the deceased or they would not get the club money. They did not complain about the man being ill. They said good night to the watchman as they Went out of the yard.—The Coroner : And you did not think it worth while to report the matter Ito the watehman.—Witness : It 1V3.8 net may business. WI. Keating was there.

LAT EST NE WS. LORD LAMINOTON. The latest bulletin about Lord Lamington is that he is still weaker to-night. DEATH OF EARL SYDNEY. Earl Sydney passed away at Frognal, Kent, yesterday morning, at one o'clock. His lordship was 85 years of age.

TEN PERSONS DROWNED IN FRANCE. A telegram from Paris, yesterday, stated that a des- patch from Pontivy says a wedding party of ten persons, including the bride and bridegroom, have been upset from a carriage into the river, all being drowned. ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE. At the Southwark Police Court, yesterday, Jessie Bevan was committed for trial on the charge of admin- istering laudanum to :her illegitimate child, and after- wards attempting to commit suicide by taking a dose of the same drug.

A PRISONER'S ATTEMPT TO ESCAPE. Henry Potter, aged 18, who had served part of a sen- tence of two months' imprisonment for larceny, leaped over a balustrade at 'Nottingham Gaol, and fell sixty feet. Both his legs and one arm were broken, and he is now lying in hospital in a precarious condition.

TERRIBLE OUTRAGE IN THE UNITED STATES. A terrible crime is reported from Crawfordsville, Arkansas, where a young lady had been outraged and murdered close to her residence. The murderer was immediately pursued and overtaken by the ° hours, who conveyed him to the scene of the outrage and hewed off his arms, legs, sand head with an axe.

SHOCKING BURNING FATALITY. On Thursday night a married woman, named Ann Gillibran, residing in Lupton-st., Bolton, was carrying a shovelful of coal upstairs to make a fire, her children being ill, when the live coal fell on her, setting fire to her clothes, which were immediately in a blaze. She rushed downstairs, and the flames were immediately extinguished, but the woman was terribly burnt, and died about midnight at the Bolton Infirmary, to which she was removed.

div.head: EMPEROR WILLIAM AND THE LABOUR
div.p: THE EMPEROR WILLIAM AND THE LABOUR

QUESTION. BERLIN, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—The Emperor opened the State Council to-day, and delivered a speech explain- ing once more his views on the Labour Question and his plans for the amelioration of the lot of the working classes. Prince Bismarck was present, and introduced the members to the Emperor. Nam, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.---4 special telegram from London states that Lord Salisbury has taken time to consider the German Government's invitation for the representation of England at the jLabour Conference at Berlin.

YESTERD A.Y'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at four o'clock. Lord Milltown introduced a Bill rendering liable to corporal punishment burglars convicted of using fire- arms. The Bill was read the first time. On the motion of Lord Dunraven, the Select Committee on the Sweating System was appointed to consider their report. This was agreed to, and the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three o'clock.

Upon the motion of Mr. RICHARD POWER, a new writ was ordered for the election of a member to serve in Parliament for the county of West Waterford, in the room of the late Mr. Douglas Pyne.
INTOXICANTS IN CLUBS.

Mr. BIGGAR then asked the !Home Secretary whether he would consider the propriety of limiting the hours for the sale of intoxicating drinks in clubs to the hours allowable in hotels and public-houses,and would attempt to carry out the limitation by legislation ? Mr. MArnimws said he was not prepared to support legisla- tion such as that suggested to be applied to bona fide clubs. The existing law operated against bogus clubs, which were really unlicensed public-houses.

THE PARNELL COMMISSION.—QUEVIONS AS TO COST. Mr. John ELLts asked the First Lord of the Treasury what was the total cost which the Government proposed the public should bear of the Special Commission, 1888, and at what time and in what manner would the sanc- tion (Atha House be asked for a vote for this sum. (Loud Liberal and Nationalist cheers).—Mr. W. L. JACKSON, the Financial Secretary to the Treasury, who answered the question,said:—l am not able to tell the hon. gentleman what the total expenditure in connection with the Special Commission has been, because some of the bills have not been examined, but as soo.l as I can get the bills I shall be glad to give the hon. gentleman the , information.

MR. PARNELL MAKES AN INQUIRY. Mr. PARNELL, rising amid loud and prolonged Nationalist cheers, said :—I beg to ask the First Lord of the Treasury what action her Majesty's Government proposes to take with reference to the report of the Special Commission appointed to inquire into the allega- tions and charges against Irish members (renewed cheer). Mr. W. H. Slims :—The report only came into the possession of her Majesty's Government last evening at ten o'clock, and they have had no opportunity of considering or determining what course shall be taken upon it.

div.head: DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.
div.p: DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.

The debate on the Address was then resumed by Mr. Parnell, who moved a long resolution condemning the unjust, exasperating, and futile administration of the present Government in Ireland, and regretting the absence from the Government programme of proposals to remedy legitimate Irish discontent. Mr. PARNELL, who was loudly cheered, declared Mr. Balfour's policy compared most unfavourably with Mr. Forster's admin- istration. He protested against the maintenance of coercion in counties where crime no longer existed, and claimed that the same measure should not be meted out to them as to blood-stained Galway and Kerry. The debate was continued by the Attorney-General for Ireland, Sir G. Trevelyan, and other members. [LIFT SITTING].

THE WARRINGTON EXTEN- SION, &c., BILL. THE PURCHASE OF THE WATERWORKS. , Yesterday the sub-committee appointed to nego- tiate upon the terms of purchase of this undertak- ing with the Water Works Committee presented their report at the meeting of the General Purposes Committee, held at the Town Hall. The report was in favour of the purchase of the undertaking upon the terms required by the Company—namely,thirty years' purchase on the maximum dividends. The compulsory provisions of the Bill will not therefore be proceeded with, and it was decided that a pub- lic meeting of the owners and ratepayers should be held at the Public Hall, next Friday evening, at half-past seven o'clock,for the purpose of considering the Bill, with the exception of the provisions in question. We understand that, if the Sinking Fund required to be established for the payment of the money to be paid to the Water Works Company is suspended for three or five years, an arrangement can be made whereby the acquisition of the Works can be effected without any serious increase of the rates. The maximum dividends of the Company upon the present capital amount to £8,025 per annum. Thirty years' purchase of that sum is £240,750, to which should be added the loan debt of the Company, £26,819. which shows a total of capital liability of £267,569. If this sum is to be paid off in sixty years, an annual payment of .£4,460 will be required, in addition to the interest of the amount of capital involved at 3± per cent., amount- ing altogether to .C 8695 per annum, making a total of £13,155. From this sum there must be deducted the revenue of the Company, which, for the year ending December last, was £8375. leaving a balance of £4,780. After further deductions for directors' fees and Company solicitors' charges, amounting to £220, which the Corporation will not have to pay, the net balance which the ratepayers will annually have to provide on this basis of Sinking Fund is £4,560, which is equivalent to a charge upon the rates of Bd. in the X. The increase in the revenue last year, over the preceding year, was £698, and for the last three years £1,629. If this rate of increase be maintained—and there is every probability that it will—at the end of three years there will be an increase in the revenue of nearly £2,000 per annum, equivalent to 4d. in the .£. Supposing, in addition, the sus- pension of the Sinking Fund to be effected, the revenue would then be equal to the amount of interest to be paid upon the capitalised sum of thirty years' purchase. so that during the period of suspension there would be no charge upon the rates. At the end of the period of;suspension, as has: been shown, the increase in the revenue might reduce the charge by 4d. in the .£. We believe that the Com- mittee have in view certain other considerations which will, it is expected, materially reduce the burden upon the rates when that time arrives. Of course, the rateable value of the Borough will be largely increased if the proposed extension comes to pass, which, so far as regards the Sinking Fund, will ease the annual contributions to be made to that fund. Broadly speaking, it may be said that the revenue from the sate of water will be sufficient to cover the interest to be paid upon the total purchase money. The only difficulty is as to paying off the capital sum by means of a sinking fund, and, as we have suggested, there are several ways in which this can be made comparatively easy to the ratepayers. It is to be hoped that a sub-committee of the General Purposes Committee will be at once appointed to consider the condition of the plant, and the general prospects of an increased revenue, with a view to being able to , assure the meeting, on Friday, that the important step which it is proposed to take has been well considered on all sides. It should be mentioned that, while still paying maximum dividends, the Waterworks Company ciuld proceed to use any sur- plus they might make for the payment of back divi- dends to the tune of £'60,000. It is of moment that . .

the ratepayers should decide to purchase before the company will be in a position to make a claim on this account, though the prospective value might be said to have been taken into consideration in the 30 years' purchase upon which it is proposed to ac- quire the undertaking. THE WARRINGTON AMATEUR MINSTREL TROVES This new minstrel organisation made a very suc- cessful start on Saturday evening, when the first public performance was given at the Cockhedge Mission room, before a crowded attendance. Messrs. Shaw, J. Bellian, and Yonge were very successful in their songs, Mr. Shaw receiving an encore for "I'll take you home again Kathleen." Messrs. liaynes, Hoult, Henry, and Westbrook were very good in several comic songs and duets, and the comic cornerman business could not have been in better hands than those of Messrs. Haynes and Henry. Mr. Stirk gave a capital solo on the cornet with the result that he had to " oblige again.' In the second part Mr. Walter Bellian gave a couple of comic songs. Mr. davenport contributed a banjo breakdown, and Mr. William Litton closed the performance by a stump speech. entitled the " Talki-phone." Si'. ANNE'S CHURCH ANNUAL TEA PARTY. On Tuesday evening the annual tea party in con- nection with St. Anne's Church, Winwick-road, was held at the schools in Dannett-st. Towards the cost of the tea, subscriptions had been received from Sir Gilbert Greenall, M.P., Lady Greenall, the Rector (Rev. F. W. Willis), •the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Francomb), the Vicar of St. Anne's (Rev. J. G. Richards), Mrs. T. IL Lyon, Mrs. Jones (The Elms), Mrs. Beamont, Miss Pierpoint, Mrs. W. Woods, Mrs. Thomas Morris, Mrs. James Wood, Mrs. Rathbone, Mis. Shillcock, J. R. Young, P. Brimelow, Henry Baker. L. Williams, and T. Cuppage. Nearly 250 members of the congregation and friends sat down to tea, and the tables were presided over by Mrs. Gibbon, Mrs. Fisher, M Ts. A. Baird, Mrs. John Baird, Mrs. Cos- grove, Miss Dooley, Miss E. Jefferson, Miss Skell and, Miss Baird, Miss Rigby, and others. The Vicar occupied the chair at the subsequent gathering, and expressed pleasure at seeing so large an attendance. It showed the interest which the congregation felt in the Church and parish, and he trusted they , would thoroughly enjoy themselves. A programme of songs and glees was then given by the choir (under the leadership of Mr. Percy Randall), and Messrs. W. Bellian, P. Randall, E. Gibbon,R. Knight J. Cosgrove, and Frederick Taylor. The acconlpani- ments were played by Miss Dooley and Mr. P. Ran- dall. Dancing afterwards took place, Mr. Frank Taylor performing the duties of M.C. darrcsixr, Practical Tailor, Bolcl-st.,Warrington.—Advt.

UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT WARRINGTON. The second of the series of Oxford University Ex- tension Lectures was delivered to the students of the Warrington Training College, on Tuesday after— noon, by Mr. 11. J. Mackinder, M.A., reader in geo- graphy in the University of Oxford. The first lec- ture WAS on the earth's crust, and that on Tuesday afternoon on "Winds." The lecturer, among other things, informed the audience that the atmosphere WaS from 40 to 50 miles iu thickness, but in the lower I 'wee miles they had half of the atmosphere. , and he might roughly say the other half in the 47 miles above. They, therefore, saw the effect of tbe..,, pressure. If they took a barometer to the top of Mont Blanc, the pressure of the air would only be one-half; that was to say that as they went UP through the atmosphere the pressure diminished Ind as they stood at one given place there W? be constant variations. There would he variationS in that room amounting to half an inch of mercury in the course of two or three days, very likely, and at the same moment the barometer at Warrington and another at Manchester would tell two different tales. The differences of pressure were due to diffe- - Irence of temperature in two wave, namely, first to hot air being lighter than cold, owing to expansionl and, secondly, to hot air holding more moistu.re than cold, and water vapour being lighter than air- - The cause of movement being difference of pressure, • the direction was governed by the relative positions of the places of low and high pressure, and to.the rotation of the earth. The cause of a draught in s room, he said, was mainly owing to the warmth of their bodies. The air came in at the bottom of a, door, flew over the room and between the bodies of the audience, and there were practically so marl tubes at work. The moving force was the warints of the bodies in the room. He wished them to re-. member that the wind was due to the difference of pressure, and that it was indeed simply a movement of air from place to place, from where the air was too crowded to where it was less crowded. IN PARMAIARNT.—SIOSION 1880. AfANCHESTER SIIIP CANAL (TIDAL OPEN- INGS, &C) BILL, AND WIDNES BRINE SUPPLY BILL. At a MEETING of the Widnes Local Board, held at the Board-room, Town Hall. Widnes. pursuant to the Act 35 and 56 Vic., c. 91, this 4th day tr: February, 1890. the above- named Bills were considered, and the following Resolutions passed, viz. : That this meeting having considered the clauses and pro- visions of a Bill intituledi " A Bill to alter ,certain works authorised by the Manchester Ship Canal Ad. 1885, and for salter purposes," it is resolved that the Local Board do oppose the said Bill in Parliament, and take all necessary steps for the due protection of the rights and interests of the district of Widnes. as represented by the Local Board for the said dis- trict ; and that the costs, charges, and expenses'incurred and to be incurred in such opposition be paid out of•the General District Fund, or out of the rates applicable to the pur- poses. That this meeting having considered the clauses and pro- visions of a Bill intituled "A Bill for incorporating and conferrhag Powers upon the Widnes Brine Supply Company, and for other purposes," it is resolved that the Local Board do oppose the said Bill in Parliament, and take all necessary steps for the due protection of the rights and interests ef the said district of Widnes, as represented by the Local Board for the said district, arid that the costs, charges. and expenses Incurred and to be incurred, in sum' opposition, be paid out of the General District Fond, or out of the rates applicable to the purpose. JAS. T. ALLEN, Clerk to the Widnes Local Board. Town Hall, Widnes, 10th February. 1890.

SHOCKING DOUBLE FATALITY. The North Lancashire Coroner has just received infor- mation of a shocking double fatality. Samuel Kendall, farmer, of Tower, was driving home from the railway elation, when the horse bolted. Kendall was thrown out and run over, dying instantly. His son David, aged nine, hearing the horse and cart on the road ran out of the farmyard to stop the animal, and was pinned between the wheel and wheel and the wall, and crushed to death. 410 - AN M.P. SHOT BY A PARAMOUR. A. well-dressed young woman, named Elizabeth Vin- cent, Was charged on Wednesday, at the Richmond Major Petty Sessions, with attempting to murder Major Isaacs, M.P. for Walworth, by shooting at him. major Isaacs admitted that he had seduced the defend ant, had been intimately acquainted with her for some • yers., and some time back made a settlement on her -91111c.1 of £2,000, £I,OOO to herself for the purpose cf go- ing.into business, and £5OO deposit on the house in ,hich she resided. In consequence of receiving a letter her he went to her house, and on entering the (lining-room she locked the door, produced a paper, and :irrith a pistol in her hand threatened to shoot him unless ne signed. He did so but refused to sign cheques which !,he demanded, and she fired, wounding him in the arm. rtiscner was remanded, bail being refused.
